/*
3256
** CAPI3REF: Memory Allocation Subsystem
3257
**
3258
** The SQLite core uses these three routines for all of its own
3259
** internal memory allocation needs. "Core" in the previous sentence
3260
** does not include operating-system specific [VFS] implementation.  The
3261
** Windows VFS uses native malloc() and free() for some operations.
3262
**
3263
** ^The sqlite3_malloc() routine returns a pointer to a block
3264
** of memory at least N bytes in length, where N is the parameter.
3265
** ^If sqlite3_malloc() is unable to obtain sufficient free
3266
** memory, it returns a NULL pointer.  ^If the parameter N to
3267
** sqlite3_malloc() is zero or negative then sqlite3_malloc() returns
3268
** a NULL pointer.
3269
**
3270
** ^The sqlite3_malloc64(N) routine works just like
3271
** sqlite3_malloc(N) except that N is an unsigned 64-bit integer instead
3272
** of a signed 32-bit integer.
3273
**
3274
** ^Calling sqlite3_free() with a pointer previously returned
3275
** by sqlite3_malloc() or sqlite3_realloc() releases that memory so
3276
** that it might be reused.  ^The sqlite3_free() routine is
3277
** a no-op if it is called with a NULL pointer.  Passing a NULL pointer
3278
** to sqlite3_free() is harmless.  After being freed, memory
3279
** should neither be read nor written.  Even reading previously freed
3280
** memory might result in a segmentation fault or other severe error.
3281
** Memory corruption, a segmentation fault, or other severe error
3282
** might result if sqlite3_free() is called with a non-NULL pointer that
3283
** was not obtained from sqlite3_malloc() or sqlite3_realloc().
3284
**
3285
** ^The sqlite3_realloc(X,N) interface attempts to resize a
3286
** prior memory allocation X to be at least N bytes.
3287
** ^If the X parameter to sqlite3_realloc(X,N)
3288
** is a NULL pointer then its behavior is identical to calling
3289
** sqlite3_malloc(N).
3290
** ^If the N parameter to sqlite3_realloc(X,N) is zero or
3291
** negative then the behavior is exactly the same as calling
3292
** sqlite3_free(X).
3293
** ^sqlite3_realloc(X,N) returns a pointer to a memory allocation
3294
** of at least N bytes in size or NULL if insufficient memory is available.
3295
** ^If M is the size of the prior allocation, then min(N,M) bytes of the
3296
** prior allocation are copied into the beginning of the buffer returned
3297
** by sqlite3_realloc(X,N) and the prior allocation is freed.
3298
** ^If sqlite3_realloc(X,N) returns NULL and N is positive, then the
3299
** prior allocation is not freed.
3300
**
3301
** ^The sqlite3_realloc64(X,N) interface works the same as
3302
** sqlite3_realloc(X,N) except that N is a 64-bit unsigned integer instead
3303
** of a 32-bit signed integer.
3304
**
3305
** ^If X is a memory allocation previously obtained from sqlite3_malloc(),
3306
** sqlite3_malloc64(), sqlite3_realloc(), or sqlite3_realloc64(), then
3307
** sqlite3_msize(X) returns the size of that memory allocation in bytes.
3308
** ^The value returned by sqlite3_msize(X) might be larger than the number
3309
** of bytes requested when X was allocated.  ^If X is a NULL pointer then
3310
** sqlite3_msize(X) returns zero.  If X points to something that is not
3311
** the beginning of memory allocation, or if it points to a formerly
3312
** valid memory allocation that has now been freed, then the behavior
3313
** of sqlite3_msize(X) is undefined and possibly harmful.
3314
**
3315
** ^The memory returned by sqlite3_malloc(), sqlite3_realloc(),
3316
** sqlite3_malloc64(), and sqlite3_realloc64()
3317
** is always aligned to at least an 8 byte boundary, or to a
3318
** 4 byte boundary if the [SQLITE_4_BYTE_ALIGNED_MALLOC] compile-time
3319
** option is used.
3320
**
3321
** The pointer arguments to [sqlite3_free()] and [sqlite3_realloc()]
3322
** must be either NULL or else pointers obtained from a prior
3323
** invocation of [sqlite3_malloc()] or [sqlite3_realloc()] that have
3324
** not yet been released.
3325
**
3326
** The application must not read or write any part of
3327
** a block of memory after it has been released using
3328
** [sqlite3_free()] or [sqlite3_realloc()].
3329
*/
3330
SQLITE_API void *sqlite3_malloc(int);
3331
SQLITE_API void *sqlite3_malloc64(sqlite3_uint64);
3332
SQLITE_API void *sqlite3_realloc(void*, int);
3333
SQLITE_API void *sqlite3_realloc64(void*, sqlite3_uint64);
3334
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_free(void*);
3335
SQLITE_API sqlite3_uint64 sqlite3_msize(void*);
3336

/*
3338
** CAPI3REF: Memory Allocator Statistics
3339
**
3340
** SQLite provides these two interfaces for reporting on the status
3341
** of the [sqlite3_malloc()], [sqlite3_free()], and [sqlite3_realloc()]
3342
** routines, which form the built-in memory allocation subsystem.
3343
**
3344
** ^The [sqlite3_memory_used()] routine returns the number of bytes
3345
** of memory currently outstanding (malloced but not freed).
3346
** ^The [sqlite3_memory_highwater()] routine returns the maximum
3347
** value of [sqlite3_memory_used()] since the high-water mark
3348
** was last reset.  ^The values returned by [sqlite3_memory_used()] and
3349
** [sqlite3_memory_highwater()] include any overhead
3350
** added by SQLite in its implementation of [sqlite3_malloc()],
3351
** but not overhead added by any underlying system library
3352
** routines that [sqlite3_malloc()] may call.
3353
**
3354
** ^The memory high-water mark is reset to the current value of
3355
** [sqlite3_memory_used()] if and only if the parameter to
3356
** [sqlite3_memory_highwater()] is true.  ^The value returned
3357
** by [sqlite3_memory_highwater(1)] is the high-water mark
3358
** prior to the reset.
3359
*/
3360
SQLITE_API sqlite3_int64 sqlite3_memory_used(void);
3361
SQLITE_API sqlite3_int64 sqlite3_memory_highwater(int resetFlag);

/*
3364
** CAPI3REF: Pseudo-Random Number Generator
3365
**
3366
** SQLite contains a high-quality pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) used to
3367
** select random [ROWID | ROWIDs] when inserting new records into a table that
3368
** already uses the largest possible [ROWID].  The PRNG is also used for
3369
** the built-in random() and randomblob() SQL functions.  This interface allows
3370
** applications to access the same PRNG for other purposes.
3371
**
3372
** ^A call to this routine stores N bytes of randomness into buffer P.
3373
** ^The P parameter can be a NULL pointer.
3374
**
3375
** ^If this routine has not been previously called or if the previous
3376
** call had N less than one or a NULL pointer for P, then the PRNG is
3377
** seeded using randomness obtained from the xRandomness method of
3378
** the default [sqlite3_vfs] object.
3379
** ^If the previous call to this routine had an N of 1 or more and a
3380
** non-NULL P then the pseudo-randomness is generated
3381
** internally and without recourse to the [sqlite3_vfs] xRandomness
3382
** method.
3383
*/
3384

/*
3387
** CAPI3REF: Compile-Time Authorization Callbacks
3388
** METHOD: sqlite3
3389
** KEYWORDS: {authorizer callback}
3390
**
3391
** ^This routine registers an authorizer callback with a particular
3392
** [database connection], supplied in the first argument.
3393
** ^The authorizer callback is invoked as SQL statements are being compiled
3394
** by [sqlite3_prepare()] or its variants [sqlite3_prepare_v2()],
3395
** [sqlite3_prepare_v3()], [sqlite3_prepare16()], [sqlite3_prepare16_v2()],
3396
** and [sqlite3_prepare16_v3()].  ^At various
3397
** points during the compilation process, as logic is being created
3398
** to perform various actions, the authorizer callback is invoked to
3399
** see if those actions are allowed.  ^The authorizer callback should
3400
** return [SQLITE_OK] to allow the action, [SQLITE_IGNORE] to disallow the
3401
** specific action but allow the SQL statement to continue to be
3402
** compiled, or [SQLITE_DENY] to cause the entire SQL statement to be
3403
** rejected with an error.  ^If the authorizer callback returns
3404
** any value other than [SQLITE_IGNORE], [SQLITE_OK], or [SQLITE_DENY]
3405
** then the [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] or equivalent call that triggered
3406
** the authorizer will fail with an error message.
3407
**
3408
** When the callback returns [SQLITE_OK], that means the operation
3409
** requested is ok.  ^When the callback returns [SQLITE_DENY], the
3410
** [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] or equivalent call that triggered the
3411
** authorizer will fail with an error message explaining that
3412
** access is denied.
3413
**
3414
** ^The first parameter to the authorizer callback is a copy of the third
3415
** parameter to the sqlite3_set_authorizer() interface. ^The second parameter
3416
** to the callback is an integer [SQLITE_READ | action code] that specifies
3417
** the particular action to be authorized. ^The third through sixth parameters
3418
** to the callback are either NULL pointers or zero-terminated strings
3419
** that contain additional details about the action to be authorized.
3420
** Applications must always be prepared to encounter a NULL pointer in any
3421
** of the third through the sixth parameters of the authorization callback.
3422
**
3423
** ^If the action code is [SQLITE_READ]
3424
** and the callback returns [SQLITE_IGNORE] then the
3425
** [prepared statement] statement is constructed to substitute
3426
** a NULL value in place of the table column that would have
3427
** been read if [SQLITE_OK] had been returned.  The [SQLITE_IGNORE]
3428
** return can be used to deny an untrusted user access to individual
3429
** columns of a table.
3430
** ^When a table is referenced by a [SELECT] but no column values are
3431
** extracted from that table (for example in a query like
3432
** "SELECT count(*) FROM tab") then the [SQLITE_READ] authorizer callback
3433
** is invoked once for that table with a column name that is an empty string.
3434
** ^If the action code is [SQLITE_DELETE] and the callback returns
3435
** [SQLITE_IGNORE] then the [DELETE] operation proceeds but the
3436
** [truncate optimization] is disabled and all rows are deleted individually.
3437
**
3438
** An authorizer is used when [sqlite3_prepare | preparing]
3439
** SQL statements from an untrusted source, to ensure that the SQL statements
3440
** do not try to access data they are not allowed to see, or that they do not
3441
** try to execute malicious statements that damage the database.  For
3442
** example, an application may allow a user to enter arbitrary
3443
** SQL queries for evaluation by a database.  But the application does
3444
** not want the user to be able to make arbitrary changes to the
3445
** database.  An authorizer could then be put in place while the
3446
** user-entered SQL is being [sqlite3_prepare | prepared] that
3447
** disallows everything except [SELECT] statements.
3448
**
3449
** Applications that need to process SQL from untrusted sources
3450
** might also consider lowering resource limits using [sqlite3_limit()]
3451
** and limiting database size using the [max_page_count] [PRAGMA]
3452
** in addition to using an authorizer.
3453
**
3454
** ^(Only a single authorizer can be in place on a database connection
3455
** at a time.  Each call to sqlite3_set_authorizer overrides the
3456
** previous call.)^  ^Disable the authorizer by installing a NULL callback.
3457
** The authorizer is disabled by default.
3458
**
3459
** <h3>Limitations And Caveats</h3><ul>
3460
**
3461
** <li>The authorizer callback must not do anything that will modify
3462
** the database connection that invoked the authorizer callback.
3463
** Note that [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] and [sqlite3_step()] both modify their
3464
** database connections for the meaning of "modify" in this paragraph.
3465
**
3466
** <li>^When [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] is used to prepare a statement, the
3467
** statement might be re-prepared during [sqlite3_step()] due to a
3468
** schema change.  Hence, the application should ensure that the
3469
** correct authorizer callback remains in place during the [sqlite3_step()].
3470
**
3471
** <li>^The authorizer callback is invoked only during
3472
** [sqlite3_prepare()] or its variants.  Authorization is not
3473
** performed during statement evaluation in [sqlite3_step()], unless
3474
** as stated in the previous paragraph, sqlite3_step() invokes
3475
** sqlite3_prepare_v2() to reprepare a statement after a schema change.
3476
**
3477
** <li>Authorizer callbacks for the expressions of a
3478
** [generated column] are invoked when the schema is parsed (and specifically
3479
** when the [CREATE TABLE] statement that contains the generated column is
3480
** parsed) not when the generated column is used in a DML statement.
3481
** This is deliberate, as one of the purposes of generated columns
3482
** is to give schema designers the ability to provide gated access
3483
** to privileged columns and/or functions.
3484
**
3485
** </ul>
3486
*/
3487
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_set_authorizer(
3488
  sqlite3*,
3489
  int (*xAuth)(void*,int,const char*,const char*,const char*,const char*),
3490
  void *pUserData
3491
);

** DEPRECATED

**

3578

** These routines register callback functions that can be used for
3581
** tracing and profiling the execution of SQL statements.

** ^The callback function registered by sqlite3_trace() is invoked at
3584

3585
** ^The sqlite3_trace() callback is invoked with a UTF-8 rendering of the
3586
** SQL statement text as the statement first begins executing.

** ^(Additional sqlite3_trace() callbacks might occur
3588
** as each triggered subprogram is entered.  The callbacks for triggers
3589
** contain a UTF-8 SQL comment that identifies the trigger.)^
3590
**
3591
** The [SQLITE_TRACE_SIZE_LIMIT] compile-time option can be used to limit
3592
** the length of [bound parameter] expansion in the output of sqlite3_trace().
3593
**
3594
** ^The callback function registered by sqlite3_profile() is invoked
3595
** as each SQL statement finishes.  ^The profile callback contains
3596
** the original statement text and an estimate of wall-clock time
3597
** of how long that statement took to run.  ^The profile callback
3598
** time is in units of nanoseconds, however the current implementation
3599
** is only capable of millisecond resolution so the six least significant
3600
** digits in the time are meaningless.  Future versions of SQLite
3601
** might provide greater resolution on the profiler callback.  Invoking
3602
** either [sqlite3_trace()] or [sqlite3_trace_v2()] will cancel the
3603
** profile callback.
3604
*/
3605

3606
   void(*xTrace)(void*,const char*), void*);

/*
3611
** CAPI3REF: SQL Trace Event Codes
3612
** KEYWORDS: SQLITE_TRACE
3613
**
3614
** These constants identify classes of events that can be monitored
3615
** using the [sqlite3_trace_v2()] tracing logic.  The M argument
3616
** to [sqlite3_trace_v2(D,M,X,P)] is an OR-ed combination of one or more of
3617
** the following constants.  ^The first argument to the trace callback
3618
** is one of the following constants.
3619
**
3620
** New tracing constants may be added in future releases.
3621
**
3622
** ^A trace callback has four arguments: xCallback(T,C,P,X).
3623
** ^The T argument is one of the integer type codes above.
3624
** ^The C argument is a copy of the context pointer passed in as the
3625
** fourth argument to [sqlite3_trace_v2()].
3626
** The P and X arguments are pointers whose meanings depend on T.
3627
**
3628
** <dl>
3629
** [[SQLITE_TRACE_STMT]] <dt>SQLITE_TRACE_STMT</dt>
3630
** <dd>^An SQLITE_TRACE_STMT callback is invoked when a prepared statement
3631
** first begins running and possibly at other times during the
3632
** execution of the prepared statement, such as at the start of each
3633
** trigger subprogram. ^The P argument is a pointer to the
3634
** [prepared statement]. ^The X argument is a pointer to a string which
3635
** is the unexpanded SQL text of the prepared statement or an SQL comment
3636
** that indicates the invocation of a trigger.  ^The callback can compute
3637
** the same text that would have been returned by the legacy [sqlite3_trace()]
3638
** interface by using the X argument when X begins with "--" and invoking
3639
** [sqlite3_expanded_sql(P)] otherwise.
3640
**
3641
** [[SQLITE_TRACE_PROFILE]] <dt>SQLITE_TRACE_PROFILE</dt>
3642
** <dd>^An SQLITE_TRACE_PROFILE callback provides approximately the same
3643
** information as is provided by the [sqlite3_profile()] callback.
3644
** ^The P argument is a pointer to the [prepared statement] and the
3645
** X argument points to a 64-bit integer which is approximately
3646
** the number of nanoseconds that the prepared statement took to run.
3647
** ^The SQLITE_TRACE_PROFILE callback is invoked when the statement finishes.
3648
**
3649
** [[SQLITE_TRACE_ROW]] <dt>SQLITE_TRACE_ROW</dt>
3650
** <dd>^An SQLITE_TRACE_ROW callback is invoked whenever a prepared
3651
** statement generates a single row of result.
3652
** ^The P argument is a pointer to the [prepared statement] and the
3653
** X argument is unused.
3654
**
3655
** [[SQLITE_TRACE_CLOSE]] <dt>SQLITE_TRACE_CLOSE</dt>
3656
** <dd>^An SQLITE_TRACE_CLOSE callback is invoked when a database
3657
** connection closes.
3658
** ^The P argument is a pointer to the [database connection] object
3659
** and the X argument is unused.
3660
** </dl>
3661
*/
3662

3663
#define SQLITE_TRACE_PROFILE    0x02
3664
#define SQLITE_TRACE_ROW        0x04
3665
#define SQLITE_TRACE_CLOSE      0x08

/*
3668
** CAPI3REF: SQL Trace Hook
3669
** METHOD: sqlite3
3670
**
3671
** ^The sqlite3_trace_v2(D,M,X,P) interface registers a trace callback
3672
** function X against [database connection] D, using property mask M
3673
** and context pointer P.  ^If the X callback is
3674
** NULL or if the M mask is zero, then tracing is disabled.  The
3675
** M argument should be the bitwise OR-ed combination of
3676
** zero or more [SQLITE_TRACE] constants.
3677
**
3678
** ^Each call to either sqlite3_trace(D,X,P) or sqlite3_trace_v2(D,M,X,P)
3679
** overrides (cancels) all prior calls to sqlite3_trace(D,X,P) or
3680
** sqlite3_trace_v2(D,M,X,P) for the [database connection] D.  Each
3681
** database connection may have at most one trace callback.
3682
**
3683
** ^The X callback is invoked whenever any of the events identified by
3684
** mask M occur.  ^The integer return value from the callback is currently
3685
** ignored, though this may change in future releases.  Callback
3686
** implementations should return zero to ensure future compatibility.
3687
**
3688
** ^A trace callback is invoked with four arguments: callback(T,C,P,X).
3689
** ^The T argument is one of the [SQLITE_TRACE]
3690
** constants to indicate why the callback was invoked.
3691
** ^The C argument is a copy of the context pointer.
3692
** The P and X arguments are pointers whose meanings depend on T.
3693
**
3694
** The sqlite3_trace_v2() interface is intended to replace the legacy
3695
** interfaces [sqlite3_trace()] and [sqlite3_profile()], both of which
3696
** are deprecated.
3697
*/
3698
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_trace_v2(
3699
  sqlite3*,
3700
  unsigned uMask,
3701
  int(*xCallback)(unsigned,void*,void*,void*),
3702
  void *pCtx
3703

/*
3706
** CAPI3REF: Query Progress Callbacks
3707
** METHOD: sqlite3
3708
**
3709
** ^The sqlite3_progress_handler(D,N,X,P) interface causes the callback
3710
** function X to be invoked periodically during long running calls to
3711
** [sqlite3_step()] and [sqlite3_prepare()] and similar for
3712
** database connection D.  An example use for this
3713
** interface is to keep a GUI updated during a large query.
3714
**
3715
** ^The parameter P is passed through as the only parameter to the
3716
** callback function X.  ^The parameter N is the approximate number of
3717
** [virtual machine instructions] that are evaluated between successive
3718
** invocations of the callback X.  ^If N is less than one then the progress
3719
** handler is disabled.
3720
**
3721
** ^Only a single progress handler may be defined at one time per
3722
** [database connection]; setting a new progress handler cancels the
3723
** old one.  ^Setting parameter X to NULL disables the progress handler.
3724
** ^The progress handler is also disabled by setting N to a value less
3725
** than 1.
3726
**
3727
** ^If the progress callback returns non-zero, the operation is
3728
** interrupted.  This feature can be used to implement a
3729
** "Cancel" button on a GUI progress dialog box.
3730
**
3731
** The progress handler callback must not do anything that will modify
3732
** the database connection that invoked the progress handler.
3733
** Note that [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] and [sqlite3_step()] both modify their
3734
** database connections for the meaning of "modify" in this paragraph.
3735
**
3736
** The progress handler callback would originally only be invoked from the
3737
** bytecode engine.  It still might be invoked during [sqlite3_prepare()]
3738
** and similar because those routines might force a reparse of the schema
3739
** which involves running the bytecode engine.  However, beginning with
3740
** SQLite version 3.41.0, the progress handler callback might also be
3741
** invoked directly from [sqlite3_prepare()] while analyzing and generating
3742
** code for complex queries.
3743
*/
3744
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_progress_handler(sqlite3*, int, int(*)(void*), void*);
3745
3746
/*
3747
** CAPI3REF: Opening A New Database Connection
3748
** CONSTRUCTOR: sqlite3
3749
**
3750
** ^These routines open an SQLite database file as specified by the
3751
** filename argument. ^The filename argument is interpreted as UTF-8 for
3752
** sqlite3_open() and sqlite3_open_v2() and as UTF-16 in the native byte
3753
** order for sqlite3_open16(). ^(A [database connection] handle is usually
3754
** returned in *ppDb, even if an error occurs.  The only exception is that
3755
** if SQLite is unable to allocate memory to hold the [sqlite3] object,
3756
** a NULL will be written into *ppDb instead of a pointer to the [sqlite3]
3757
** object.)^ ^(If the database is opened (and/or created) successfully, then
3758
** [SQLITE_OK] is returned.  Otherwise an [error code] is returned.)^ ^The
3759
** [sqlite3_errmsg()] or [sqlite3_errmsg16()] routines can be used to obtain
3760
** an English language description of the error following a failure of any
3761
** of the sqlite3_open() routines.
3762
**
3763
** ^The default encoding will be UTF-8 for databases created using
3764
** sqlite3_open() or sqlite3_open_v2().  ^The default encoding for databases
3765
** created using sqlite3_open16() will be UTF-16 in the native byte order.
3766
**
3767
** Whether or not an error occurs when it is opened, resources
3768
** associated with the [database connection] handle should be released by
3769
** passing it to [sqlite3_close()] when it is no longer required.
3770
**
3771
** The sqlite3_open_v2() interface works like sqlite3_open()
3772
** except that it accepts two additional parameters for additional control
3773
** over the new database connection.  ^(The flags parameter to
3774
** sqlite3_open_v2() must include, at a minimum, one of the following
3775
** three flag combinations:)^
3776
**
3777
** <dl>
3778
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY]</dt>
3779
** <dd>The database is opened in read-only mode.  If the database does
3780
** not already exist, an error is returned.</dd>)^
3781
**
3782
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE]</dt>
3783
** <dd>The database is opened for reading and writing if possible, or
3784
** reading only if the file is write protected by the operating
3785
** system.  In either case the database must already exist, otherwise
3786
** an error is returned.  For historical reasons, if opening in
3787
** read-write mode fails due to OS-level permissions, an attempt is
3788
** made to open it in read-only mode. [sqlite3_db_readonly()] can be
3789
** used to determine whether the database is actually
3790
** read-write.</dd>)^
3791
**
3792
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE] | [SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE]</dt>
3793
** <dd>The database is opened for reading and writing, and is created if
3794
** it does not already exist. This is the behavior that is always used for
3795
** sqlite3_open() and sqlite3_open16().</dd>)^
3796
** </dl>
3797
**
3798
** In addition to the required flags, the following optional flags are
3799
** also supported:
3800
**
3801
** <dl>
3802
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_URI]</dt>
3803
** <dd>The filename can be interpreted as a URI if this flag is set.</dd>)^
3804
**
3805
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_MEMORY]</dt>
3806
** <dd>The database will be opened as an in-memory database.  The database
3807
** is named by the "filename" argument for the purposes of cache-sharing,
3808
** if shared cache mode is enabled, but the "filename" is otherwise ignored.
3809
** </dd>)^
3810
**
3811
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_NOMUTEX]</dt>
3812
** <dd>The new database connection will use the "multi-thread"
3813
** [threading mode].)^  This means that separate threads are allowed
3814
** to use SQLite at the same time, as long as each thread is using
3815
** a different [database connection].
3816
**
3817
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_FULLMUTEX]</dt>
3818
** <dd>The new database connection will use the "serialized"
3819
** [threading mode].)^  This means the multiple threads can safely
3820
** attempt to use the same database connection at the same time.
3821
** (Mutexes will block any actual concurrency, but in this mode
3822
** there is no harm in trying.)
3823
**
3824
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_SHAREDCACHE]</dt>
3825
** <dd>The database is opened with [shared cache] enabled, overriding
3826
** the default shared cache setting provided by
3827
** [sqlite3_enable_shared_cache()].)^
3828
** The [use of shared cache mode is discouraged] and hence shared cache
3829
** capabilities may be omitted from many builds of SQLite.  In such cases,
3830
** this option is a no-op.
3831
**
3832
** ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_PRIVATECACHE]</dt>
3833
** <dd>The database is opened with [shared cache] disabled, overriding
3834
** the default shared cache setting provided by
3835
** [sqlite3_enable_shared_cache()].)^
3836
**
3837
** [[OPEN_EXRESCODE]] ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_EXRESCODE]</dt>
3838
** <dd>The database connection comes up in "extended result code mode".
3839
** In other words, the database behaves as if
3840
** [sqlite3_extended_result_codes(db,1)] were called on the database
3841
** connection as soon as the connection is created. In addition to setting
3842
** the extended result code mode, this flag also causes [sqlite3_open_v2()]
3843
** to return an extended result code.</dd>
3844
**
3845
** [[OPEN_NOFOLLOW]] ^(<dt>[SQLITE_OPEN_NOFOLLOW]</dt>
3846
** <dd>The database filename is not allowed to contain a symbolic link</dd>
3847
** </dl>)^
3848
**
3849
** If the 3rd parameter to sqlite3_open_v2() is not one of the
3850
** required combinations shown above optionally combined with other
3851
** [SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY | SQLITE_OPEN_* bits]
3852
** then the behavior is undefined.  Historic versions of SQLite
3853
** have silently ignored surplus bits in the flags parameter to
3854
** sqlite3_open_v2(), however that behavior might not be carried through
3855
** into future versions of SQLite and so applications should not rely
3856
** upon it.  Note in particular that the SQLITE_OPEN_EXCLUSIVE flag is a no-op
3857
** for sqlite3_open_v2().  The SQLITE_OPEN_EXCLUSIVE does *not* cause
3858
** the open to fail if the database already exists.  The SQLITE_OPEN_EXCLUSIVE
3859
** flag is intended for use by the [sqlite3_vfs|VFS interface] only, and not
3860
** by sqlite3_open_v2().
3861
**
3862
** ^The fourth parameter to sqlite3_open_v2() is the name of the
3863
** [sqlite3_vfs] object that defines the operating system interface that
3864
** the new database connection should use.  ^If the fourth parameter is
3865
** a NULL pointer then the default [sqlite3_vfs] object is used.
3866
**
3867
** ^If the filename is ":memory:", then a private, temporary in-memory database
3868
** is created for the connection.  ^This in-memory database will vanish when
3869
** the database connection is closed.  Future versions of SQLite might
3870
** make use of additional special filenames that begin with the ":" character.
3871
** It is recommended that when a database filename actually does begin with
3872
** a ":" character you should prefix the filename with a pathname such as
3873
** "./" to avoid ambiguity.
3874
**
3875
** ^If the filename is an empty string, then a private, temporary
3876
** on-disk database will be created.  ^This private database will be
3877
** automatically deleted as soon as the database connection is closed.
3878
**
3879
** [[URI filenames in sqlite3_open()]] <h3>URI Filenames</h3>
3880
**
3881
** ^If [URI filename] interpretation is enabled, and the filename argument
3882
** begins with "file:", then the filename is interpreted as a URI. ^URI
3883
** filename interpretation is enabled if the [SQLITE_OPEN_URI] flag is
3884
** set in the third argument to sqlite3_open_v2(), or if it has
3885
** been enabled globally using the [SQLITE_CONFIG_URI] option with the
3886
** [sqlite3_config()] method or by the [SQLITE_USE_URI] compile-time option.
3887
** URI filename interpretation is turned off
3888
** by default, but future releases of SQLite might enable URI filename
3889
** interpretation by default.  See "[URI filenames]" for additional
3890
** information.
3891
**
3892
** URI filenames are parsed according to RFC 3986. ^If the URI contains an
3893
** authority, then it must be either an empty string or the string
3894
** "localhost". ^If the authority is not an empty string or "localhost", an
3895
** error is returned to the caller. ^The fragment component of a URI, if
3896
** present, is ignored.
3897
**
3898
** ^SQLite uses the path component of the URI as the name of the disk file
3899
** which contains the database. ^If the path begins with a '/' character,
3900
** then it is interpreted as an absolute path. ^If the path does not begin
3901
** with a '/' (meaning that the authority section is omitted from the URI)
3902
** then the path is interpreted as a relative path.
3903
** ^(On windows, the first component of an absolute path
3904
** is a drive specification (e.g. "C:").)^
3905
**
3906
** [[core URI query parameters]]
3907
** The query component of a URI may contain parameters that are interpreted
3908
** either by SQLite itself, or by a [VFS | custom VFS implementation].
3909
** SQLite and its built-in [VFSes] interpret the
3910
** following query parameters:
3911
**
3912
** <ul>
3913
**   <li> <b>vfs</b>: ^The "vfs" parameter may be used to specify the name of
3914
**     a VFS object that provides the operating system interface that should
3915
**     be used to access the database file on disk. ^If this option is set to
3916
**     an empty string the default VFS object is used. ^Specifying an unknown
3917
**     VFS is an error. ^If sqlite3_open_v2() is used and the vfs option is
3918
**     present, then the VFS specified by the option takes precedence over
3919
**     the value passed as the fourth parameter to sqlite3_open_v2().
3920
**
3921
**   <li> <b>mode</b>: ^(The mode parameter may be set to either "ro", "rw",
3922
**     "rwc", or "memory". Attempting to set it to any other value is
3923
**     an error)^.
3924
**     ^If "ro" is specified, then the database is opened for read-only
3925
**     access, just as if the [SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY] flag had been set in the
3926
**     third argument to sqlite3_open_v2(). ^If the mode option is set to
3927
**     "rw", then the database is opened for read-write (but not create)
3928
**     access, as if SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE (but not SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE) had
3929
**     been set. ^Value "rwc" is equivalent to setting both
3930
**     SQLITE_OPEN_READWRITE and SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE.  ^If the mode option is
3931
**     set to "memory" then a pure [in-memory database] that never reads
3932
**     or writes from disk is used. ^It is an error to specify a value for
3933
**     the mode parameter that is less restrictive than that specified by
3934
**     the flags passed in the third parameter to sqlite3_open_v2().
3935
**
3936
**   <li> <b>cache</b>: ^The cache parameter may be set to either "shared" or
3937
**     "private". ^Setting it to "shared" is equivalent to setting the
3938
**     SQLITE_OPEN_SHAREDCACHE bit in the flags argument passed to
3939
**     sqlite3_open_v2(). ^Setting the cache parameter to "private" is
3940
**     equivalent to setting the SQLITE_OPEN_PRIVATECACHE bit.
3941
**     ^If sqlite3_open_v2() is used and the "cache" parameter is present in
3942
**     a URI filename, its value overrides any behavior requested by setting
3943
**     SQLITE_OPEN_PRIVATECACHE or SQLITE_OPEN_SHAREDCACHE flag.
3944
**
3945
**  <li> <b>psow</b>: ^The psow parameter indicates whether or not the
3946
**     [powersafe overwrite] property does or does not apply to the
3947
**     storage media on which the database file resides.
3948
**
3949
**  <li> <b>nolock</b>: ^The nolock parameter is a boolean query parameter
3950
**     which if set disables file locking in rollback journal modes.  This
3951
**     is useful for accessing a database on a filesystem that does not
3952
**     support locking.  Caution:  Database corruption might result if two
3953
**     or more processes write to the same database and any one of those
3954
**     processes uses nolock=1.
3955
**
3956
**  <li> <b>immutable</b>: ^The immutable parameter is a boolean query
3957
**     parameter that indicates that the database file is stored on
3958
**     read-only media.  ^When immutable is set, SQLite assumes that the
3959
**     database file cannot be changed, even by a process with higher
3960
**     privilege, and so the database is opened read-only and all locking
3961
**     and change detection is disabled.  Caution: Setting the immutable
3962
**     property on a database file that does in fact change can result
3963
**     in incorrect query results and/or [SQLITE_CORRUPT] errors.
3964
**     See also: [SQLITE_IOCAP_IMMUTABLE].
3965
**
3966
** </ul>
3967
**
3968
** ^Specifying an unknown parameter in the query component of a URI is not an
3969
** error.  Future versions of SQLite might understand additional query
3970
** parameters.  See "[query parameters with special meaning to SQLite]" for
3971
** additional information.
3972
**
3973
** [[URI filename examples]] <h3>URI filename examples</h3>
3974
**
3975
** <table border="1" align=center cellpadding=5>
3976
** <tr><th> URI filenames <th> Results
3977
** <tr><td> file:data.db <td>
3978
**          Open the file "data.db" in the current directory.
3979
** <tr><td> file:/home/fred/data.db<br>
3980
**          file:///home/fred/data.db <br>
3981
**          file://localhost/home/fred/data.db <br> <td>
3982
**          Open the database file "/home/fred/data.db".
3983
** <tr><td> file://darkstar/home/fred/data.db <td>
3984
**          An error. "darkstar" is not a recognized authority.
3985
** <tr><td style="white-space:nowrap">
3986
**          file:///C:/Documents%20and%20Settings/fred/Desktop/data.db
3987
**     <td> Windows only: Open the file "data.db" on fred's desktop on drive
3988
**          C:. Note that the %20 escaping in this example is not strictly
3989
**          necessary - space characters can be used literally
3990
**          in URI filenames.
3991
** <tr><td> file:data.db?mode=ro&cache=private <td>
3992
**          Open file "data.db" in the current directory for read-only access.
3993
**          Regardless of whether or not shared-cache mode is enabled by
3994
**          default, use a private cache.
3995
** <tr><td> file:/home/fred/data.db?vfs=unix-dotfile <td>
3996
**          Open file "/home/fred/data.db". Use the special VFS "unix-dotfile"
3997
**          that uses dot-files in place of posix advisory locking.
3998
** <tr><td> file:data.db?mode=readonly <td>
3999
**          An error. "readonly" is not a valid option for the "mode" parameter.
4000
**          Use "ro" instead:  "file:data.db?mode=ro".
4001
** </table>
4002
**
4003
** ^URI hexadecimal escape sequences (%HH) are supported within the path and
4004
** query components of a URI. A hexadecimal escape sequence consists of a
4005
** percent sign - "%" - followed by exactly two hexadecimal digits
4006
** specifying an octet value. ^Before the path or query components of a
4007
** URI filename are interpreted, they are encoded using UTF-8 and all
4008
** hexadecimal escape sequences replaced by a single byte containing the
4009
** corresponding octet. If this process generates an invalid UTF-8 encoding,
4010
** the results are undefined.
4011
**
4012
** <b>Note to Windows users:</b>  The encoding used for the filename argument
4013
** of sqlite3_open() and sqlite3_open_v2() must be UTF-8, not whatever
4014
** codepage is currently defined.  Filenames containing international
4015
** characters must be converted to UTF-8 prior to passing them into
4016
** sqlite3_open() or sqlite3_open_v2().
4017
**
4018
** <b>Note to Windows Runtime users:</b>  The temporary directory must be set
4019
** prior to calling sqlite3_open() or sqlite3_open_v2().  Otherwise, various
4020
** features that require the use of temporary files may fail.
4021
**
4022
** See also: [sqlite3_temp_directory]
4023
*/
4024
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_open(
4025
  const char *filename,   /* Database filename (UTF-8) */
4026
  sqlite3 **ppDb          /* OUT: SQLite db handle */
4027
);
4028
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_open16(
4029
  const void *filename,   /* Database filename (UTF-16) */
4030
  sqlite3 **ppDb          /* OUT: SQLite db handle */
4031
);
4032
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_open_v2(
4033
  const char *filename,   /* Database filename (UTF-8) */
4034
  sqlite3 **ppDb,         /* OUT: SQLite db handle */
4035
  int flags,              /* Flags */
4036
  const char *zVfs        /* Name of VFS module to use */
4037
);
4038
4039
/*
4040
** CAPI3REF: Obtain Values For URI Parameters
4041
**
4042
** These are utility routines, useful to [VFS|custom VFS implementations],
4043
** that check if a database file was a URI that contained a specific query
4044
** parameter, and if so obtains the value of that query parameter.
4045
**
4046
** The first parameter to these interfaces (hereafter referred to
4047
** as F) must be one of:
4048
** <ul>
4049
** <li> A database filename pointer created by the SQLite core and
4050
** passed into the xOpen() method of a VFS implementation, or
4051
** <li> A filename obtained from [sqlite3_db_filename()], or
4052
** <li> A new filename constructed using [sqlite3_create_filename()].
4053
** </ul>
4054
** If the F parameter is not one of the above, then the behavior is
4055
** undefined and probably undesirable.  Older versions of SQLite were
4056
** more tolerant of invalid F parameters than newer versions.
4057
**
4058
** If F is a suitable filename (as described in the previous paragraph)
4059
** and if P is the name of the query parameter, then
4060
** sqlite3_uri_parameter(F,P) returns the value of the P
4061
** parameter if it exists or a NULL pointer if P does not appear as a
4062
** query parameter on F.  If P is a query parameter of F and it
4063
** has no explicit value, then sqlite3_uri_parameter(F,P) returns
4064
** a pointer to an empty string.
4065
**
4066
** The sqlite3_uri_boolean(F,P,B) routine assumes that P is a boolean
4067
** parameter and returns true (1) or false (0) according to the value
4068
** of P.  The sqlite3_uri_boolean(F,P,B) routine returns true (1) if the
4069
** value of query parameter P is one of "yes", "true", or "on" in any
4070
** case or if the value begins with a non-zero number.  The
4071
** sqlite3_uri_boolean(F,P,B) routines returns false (0) if the value of
4072
** query parameter P is one of "no", "false", or "off" in any case or
4073
** if the value begins with a numeric zero.  If P is not a query
4074
** parameter on F or if the value of P does not match any of the
4075
** above, then sqlite3_uri_boolean(F,P,B) returns (B!=0).
4076
**
4077
** The sqlite3_uri_int64(F,P,D) routine converts the value of P into a
4078
** 64-bit signed integer and returns that integer, or D if P does not
4079
** exist or ff the value of P is something other than an integer.
4080
**
4081
** The sqlite3_uri_key(F,N) returns a pointer to the name (not
4082
** the value) of the N-th query parameter for filename F, or a NULL
4083
** pointer if N is less than zero or greater than the number of query
4084
** parameters minus 1.  The N value is zero-based so N should be 0 to obtain
4085
** the name of the first query parameter, 1 for the second parameter, and
4086
** so forth.
4087
**
4088
** If F is a NULL pointer, then sqlite3_uri_parameter(F,P) returns NULL and
4089
** sqlite3_uri_boolean(F,P,B) returns B.  If F is not a NULL pointer and
4090
** is not a database file pathname pointer that the SQLite core passed
4091
** into the xOpen VFS method, then the behavior of this routine is undefined
4092
** and probably undesirable.
4093
**
4094
** Beginning with SQLite [version 3.31.0] ([dateof:3.31.0]) the input F
4095
** parameter can also be the name of a rollback journal file or WAL file
4096
** in addition to the main database file.  Prior to version 3.31.0, these
4097
** routines would only work if F was the name of the main database file.
4098
** When the F parameter is the name of the rollback journal or WAL file,
4099
** it has access to all the same query parameters as were found on the
4100
** main database file.
4101
**
4102
** See the [URI filename] documentation for additional information.
4103
*/
4104
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_uri_parameter(sqlite3_filename z, const char *zParam);
4105
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_uri_boolean(sqlite3_filename z, const char *zParam, int bDefault);
4106
SQLITE_API sqlite3_int64 sqlite3_uri_int64(sqlite3_filename, const char*, sqlite3_int64);
4107
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_uri_key(sqlite3_filename z, int N);
4108
4109
/*
4110
** CAPI3REF:  Translate filenames
4111
**
4112
** These routines are available to [VFS|custom VFS implementations] for
4113
** translating filenames between the main database file, the journal file,
4114
** and the WAL file.
4115
**
4116
** If F is the name of an sqlite database file, journal file, or WAL file
4117
** passed by the SQLite core into the VFS, then sqlite3_filename_database(F)
4118
** returns the name of the corresponding database file.
4119
**
4120
** If F is the name of an sqlite database file, journal file, or WAL file
4121
** passed by the SQLite core into the VFS, or if F is a database filename
4122
** obtained from [sqlite3_db_filename()], then sqlite3_filename_journal(F)
4123
** returns the name of the corresponding rollback journal file.
4124
**
4125
** If F is the name of an sqlite database file, journal file, or WAL file
4126
** that was passed by the SQLite core into the VFS, or if F is a database
4127
** filename obtained from [sqlite3_db_filename()], then
4128
** sqlite3_filename_wal(F) returns the name of the corresponding
4129
** WAL file.
4130
**
4131
** In all of the above, if F is not the name of a database, journal or WAL
4132
** filename passed into the VFS from the SQLite core and F is not the
4133
** return value from [sqlite3_db_filename()], then the result is
4134
** undefined and is likely a memory access violation.
4135
*/
4136
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_filename_database(sqlite3_filename);
4137
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_filename_journal(sqlite3_filename);
4138
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_filename_wal(sqlite3_filename);
4139
4140
/*
4141
** CAPI3REF:  Database File Corresponding To A Journal
4142
**
4143
** ^If X is the name of a rollback or WAL-mode journal file that is
4144
** passed into the xOpen method of [sqlite3_vfs], then
4145
** sqlite3_database_file_object(X) returns a pointer to the [sqlite3_file]
4146
** object that represents the main database file.
4147
**
4148
** This routine is intended for use in custom [VFS] implementations
4149
** only.  It is not a general-purpose interface.
4150
** The argument sqlite3_file_object(X) must be a filename pointer that
4151
** has been passed into [sqlite3_vfs].xOpen method where the
4152
** flags parameter to xOpen contains one of the bits
4153
** [SQLITE_OPEN_MAIN_JOURNAL] or [SQLITE_OPEN_WAL].  Any other use
4154
** of this routine results in undefined and probably undesirable
4155
** behavior.
4156
*/
4157
SQLITE_API sqlite3_file *sqlite3_database_file_object(const char*);
4158
4159
/*
4160
** CAPI3REF: Create and Destroy VFS Filenames
4161
**
4162
** These interfaces are provided for use by [VFS shim] implementations and
4163
** are not useful outside of that context.
4164
**
4165
** The sqlite3_create_filename(D,J,W,N,P) allocates memory to hold a version of
4166
** database filename D with corresponding journal file J and WAL file W and
4167
** an array P of N URI Key/Value pairs.  The result from
4168
** sqlite3_create_filename(D,J,W,N,P) is a pointer to a database filename that
4169
** is safe to pass to routines like:
4170
** <ul>
4171
** <li> [sqlite3_uri_parameter()],
4172
** <li> [sqlite3_uri_boolean()],
4173
** <li> [sqlite3_uri_int64()],
4174
** <li> [sqlite3_uri_key()],
4175
** <li> [sqlite3_filename_database()],
4176
** <li> [sqlite3_filename_journal()], or
4177
** <li> [sqlite3_filename_wal()].
4178
** </ul>
4179
** If a memory allocation error occurs, sqlite3_create_filename() might
4180
** return a NULL pointer.  The memory obtained from sqlite3_create_filename(X)
4181
** must be released by a corresponding call to sqlite3_free_filename(Y).
4182
**
4183
** The P parameter in sqlite3_create_filename(D,J,W,N,P) should be an array
4184
** of 2*N pointers to strings.  Each pair of pointers in this array corresponds
4185
** to a key and value for a query parameter.  The P parameter may be a NULL
4186
** pointer if N is zero.  None of the 2*N pointers in the P array may be
4187
** NULL pointers and key pointers should not be empty strings.
4188
** None of the D, J, or W parameters to sqlite3_create_filename(D,J,W,N,P) may
4189
** be NULL pointers, though they can be empty strings.
4190
**
4191
** The sqlite3_free_filename(Y) routine releases a memory allocation
4192
** previously obtained from sqlite3_create_filename().  Invoking
4193
** sqlite3_free_filename(Y) where Y is a NULL pointer is a harmless no-op.
4194
**
4195
** If the Y parameter to sqlite3_free_filename(Y) is anything other
4196
** than a NULL pointer or a pointer previously acquired from
4197
** sqlite3_create_filename(), then bad things such as heap
4198
** corruption or segfaults may occur. The value Y should not be
4199
** used again after sqlite3_free_filename(Y) has been called.  This means
4200
** that if the [sqlite3_vfs.xOpen()] method of a VFS has been called using Y,
4201
** then the corresponding [sqlite3_module.xClose() method should also be
4202
** invoked prior to calling sqlite3_free_filename(Y).
4203
*/
4204
SQLITE_API sqlite3_filename sqlite3_create_filename(
4205
  const char *zDatabase,
4206
  const char *zJournal,
4207
  const char *zWal,
4208
  int nParam,
4209
  const char **azParam
4210
);
4211
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_free_filename(sqlite3_filename);
4212
4213
/*
4214
** CAPI3REF: Error Codes And Messages
4215
** METHOD: sqlite3
4216
**
4217
** ^If the most recent sqlite3_* API call associated with
4218
** [database connection] D failed, then the sqlite3_errcode(D) interface
4219
** returns the numeric [result code] or [extended result code] for that
4220
** API call.
4221
** ^The sqlite3_extended_errcode()
4222
** interface is the same except that it always returns the
4223
** [extended result code] even when extended result codes are
4224
** disabled.
4225
**
4226
** The values returned by sqlite3_errcode() and/or
4227
** sqlite3_extended_errcode() might change with each API call.
4228
** Except, there are some interfaces that are guaranteed to never
4229
** change the value of the error code.  The error-code preserving
4230
** interfaces include the following:
4231
**
4232
** <ul>
4233
** <li> sqlite3_errcode()
4234
** <li> sqlite3_extended_errcode()
4235
** <li> sqlite3_errmsg()
4236
** <li> sqlite3_errmsg16()
4237
** <li> sqlite3_error_offset()
4238
** <li> sqlite3_db_handle()
4239
** </ul>
4240
**
4241
** ^The sqlite3_errmsg() and sqlite3_errmsg16() return English-language
4242
** text that describes the error, as either UTF-8 or UTF-16 respectively,
4243
** or NULL if no error message is available.
4244
** (See how SQLite handles [invalid UTF] for exceptions to this rule.)
4245
** ^(Memory to hold the error message string is managed internally.
4246
** The application does not need to worry about freeing the result.
4247
** However, the error string might be overwritten or deallocated by
4248
** subsequent calls to other SQLite interface functions.)^
4249
**
4250
** ^The sqlite3_errstr(E) interface returns the English-language text
4251
** that describes the [result code] E, as UTF-8, or NULL if E is not a
4252
** result code for which a text error message is available.
4253
** ^(Memory to hold the error message string is managed internally
4254
** and must not be freed by the application)^.
4255
**
4256
** ^If the most recent error references a specific token in the input
4257
** SQL, the sqlite3_error_offset() interface returns the byte offset
4258
** of the start of that token.  ^The byte offset returned by
4259
** sqlite3_error_offset() assumes that the input SQL is UTF-8.
4260
** ^If the most recent error does not reference a specific token in the input
4261
** SQL, then the sqlite3_error_offset() function returns -1.
4262
**
4263
** When the serialized [threading mode] is in use, it might be the
4264
** case that a second error occurs on a separate thread in between
4265
** the time of the first error and the call to these interfaces.
4266
** When that happens, the second error will be reported since these
4267
** interfaces always report the most recent result.  To avoid
4268
** this, each thread can obtain exclusive use of the [database connection] D
4269
** by invoking [sqlite3_mutex_enter]([sqlite3_db_mutex](D)) before beginning
4270
** to use D and invoking [sqlite3_mutex_leave]([sqlite3_db_mutex](D)) after
4271
** all calls to the interfaces listed here are completed.
4272
**
4273
** If an interface fails with SQLITE_MISUSE, that means the interface
4274
** was invoked incorrectly by the application.  In that case, the
4275
** error code and message may or may not be set.
4276
*/
4277
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_errcode(sqlite3 *db);
4278
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_extended_errcode(sqlite3 *db);
4279
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_errmsg(sqlite3*);
4280
SQLITE_API const void *sqlite3_errmsg16(sqlite3*);
4281
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_errstr(int);
4282
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_error_offset(sqlite3 *db);

4285
** CAPI3REF: Set Error Code And Message
4286
** METHOD: sqlite3
4287
**
4288

4289
** to errcode, and the error message to a copy of nul-terminated string
4290
** zErrMsg. If zErrMsg is passed NULL, then the error message is set to
4291
** the default message associated with the supplied error code.  Subsequent
4292
** calls to [sqlite3_errcode()] and [sqlite3_errmsg()] and similar will
4293
** return the values set by this routine in place of what was previously
4294
** set by SQLite itself.
4295
**
4296
** This function returns SQLITE_OK if the error code and error message are
4297
** successfully set, SQLITE_NOMEM if an OOM occurs, and SQLITE_MISUSE if
4298
** the database handle is NULL or invalid.
4299
**
4300
** The error code and message set by this routine remains in effect until
4301
** they are changed, either by another call to this routine or until they are
4302
** changed to by SQLite itself to reflect the result of some subsquent
4303
** API call.
4304
**
4305
** This function is intended for use by SQLite extensions or wrappers.  The
4306
** idea is that an extension or wrapper can use this routine to set error
4307
** messages and error codes and thus behave more like a core SQLite
4308
** feature from the point of view of an application.
4309
*/
4310
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_set_errmsg(sqlite3 *db, int errcode, const char *zErrMsg);

/*
4313
** CAPI3REF: Prepared Statement Object
4314
** KEYWORDS: {prepared statement} {prepared statements}
4315
**
4316
** An instance of this object represents a single SQL statement that
4317
** has been compiled into binary form and is ready to be evaluated.
4318
**
4319
** Think of each SQL statement as a separate computer program.  The
4320
** original SQL text is source code.  A prepared statement object
4321
** is the compiled object code.  All SQL must be converted into a
4322
** prepared statement before it can be run.
4323
**
4324
** The life-cycle of a prepared statement object usually goes like this:
4325
**
4326
** <ol>
4327
** <li> Create the prepared statement object using [sqlite3_prepare_v2()].
4328
** <li> Bind values to [parameters] using the sqlite3_bind_*()
4329
**      interfaces.
4330
** <li> Run the SQL by calling [sqlite3_step()] one or more times.
4331
** <li> Reset the prepared statement using [sqlite3_reset()] then go back
4332
**      to step 2.  Do this zero or more times.
4333
** <li> Destroy the object using [sqlite3_finalize()].
4334
** </ol>
4335
*/
4336
typedef struct sqlite3_stmt sqlite3_stmt;

/*
4339
** CAPI3REF: Run-time Limits
4340
** METHOD: sqlite3
4341
**
4342
** ^(This interface allows the size of various constructs to be limited
4343
** on a connection by connection basis.  The first parameter is the
4344
** [database connection] whose limit is to be set or queried.  The
4345
** second parameter is one of the [limit categories] that define a
4346
** class of constructs to be size limited.  The third parameter is the
4347
** new limit for that construct.)^
4348
**
4349
** ^If the new limit is a negative number, the limit is unchanged.
4350
** ^(For each limit category SQLITE_LIMIT_<i>NAME</i> there is a
4351
** [limits | hard upper bound]
4352
** set at compile-time by a C preprocessor macro called
4353
** [limits | SQLITE_MAX_<i>NAME</i>].
4354
** (The "_LIMIT_" in the name is changed to "_MAX_".))^
4355
** ^Attempts to increase a limit above its hard upper bound are
4356
** silently truncated to the hard upper bound.
4357
**
4358
** ^Regardless of whether or not the limit was changed, the
4359
** [sqlite3_limit()] interface returns the prior value of the limit.
4360
** ^Hence, to find the current value of a limit without changing it,
4361
** simply invoke this interface with the third parameter set to -1.
4362
**
4363
** Run-time limits are intended for use in applications that manage
4364
** both their own internal database and also databases that are controlled
4365
** by untrusted external sources.  An example application might be a
4366
** web browser that has its own databases for storing history and
4367
** separate databases controlled by JavaScript applications downloaded
4368
** off the Internet.  The internal databases can be given the
4369
** large, default limits.  Databases managed by external sources can
4370
** be given much smaller limits designed to prevent a denial of service
4371
** attack.  Developers might also want to use the [sqlite3_set_authorizer()]
4372
** interface to further control untrusted SQL.  The size of the database
4373
** created by an untrusted script can be contained using the
4374
** [max_page_count] [PRAGMA].
4375
**
4376
** New run-time limit categories may be added in future releases.
4377
*/
4378
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_limit(sqlite3*, int id, int newVal);

**
4384
** These constants define various performance limits
4385
** that can be lowered at run-time using [sqlite3_limit()].
4386
** A concise description of these limits follows, and additional information
4387
** is available at [limits | Limits in SQLite].
4388
**
4389
** <dl>
4390
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH</dt>
4391
** <dd>The maximum size of any string or BLOB or table row, in bytes.<dd>)^
4392
**
4393
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH</dt>
4394
** <dd>The maximum length of an SQL statement, in bytes.</dd>)^
4395
**
4396
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_COLUMN]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_COLUMN</dt>
4397

4398
** result set of a [SELECT] or the maximum number of columns in an index
4399
** or in an ORDER BY or GROUP BY clause.</dd>)^
4400
**
4401
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_EXPR_DEPTH]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_EXPR_DEPTH</dt>
4402
** <dd>The maximum depth of the parse tree on any expression and
4403
** the maximum nesting depth for subqueries and VIEWs</dd>)^

**

** <dd>The maximum depth of the LALR(1) parser stack used to analyze
4407
** input SQL statements.</dd>)^
4408
**
4409
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_COMPOUND_SELECT]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_COMPOUND_SELECT</dt>
4410
** <dd>The maximum number of terms in a compound SELECT statement.</dd>)^
4411
**
4412
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_VDBE_OP]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_VDBE_OP</dt>

** <dd>The maximum number of instructions in a virtual machine program
4414

4415
** the equivalent tries to allocate space for more than this many opcodes
4416
** in a single prepared statement, an SQLITE_NOMEM error is returned.</dd>)^
4417
**
4418
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_FUNCTION_ARG]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_FUNCTION_ARG</dt>
4419
** <dd>The maximum number of arguments on a function.</dd>)^
4420
**
4421
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED</dt>
4422
** <dd>The maximum number of [ATTACH | attached databases].)^</dd>
4423
**
4424
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_LIKE_PATTERN_LENGTH]]
4425
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_LIKE_PATTERN_LENGTH</dt>
4426
** <dd>The maximum length of the pattern argument to the [LIKE] or
4427
** [GLOB] operators.</dd>)^
4428
**
4429
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER]]
4430
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER</dt>
4431
** <dd>The maximum index number of any [parameter] in an SQL statement.)^
4432
**
4433
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_DEPTH]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_TRIGGER_DEPTH</dt>
4434
** <dd>The maximum depth of recursion for triggers, and the maximum
4435
** nesting depth for separate triggers.</dd>)^
4436
**
4437
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_WORKER_THREADS]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_WORKER_THREADS</dt>
4438
** <dd>The maximum number of auxiliary worker threads that a single
4439
** [prepared statement] may start.</dd>)^
4440
**
4441
** [[SQLITE_LIMIT_SCHEMA]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_LIMIT_SCHEMA</dt>
4442
** <dd>The maximum number of objects (tables, indexes, triggers, and views)
4443

**

/*
4467
** CAPI3REF: Prepare Flags
4468
**
4469
** These constants define various flags that can be passed into the
4470
** "prepFlags" parameter of the [sqlite3_prepare_v3()] and
4471
** [sqlite3_prepare16_v3()] interfaces.
4472
**
4473
** New flags may be added in future releases of SQLite.
4474
**
4475
** <dl>
4476
** [[SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT</dt>
4477
** <dd>The SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT flag is a hint to the query planner
4478
** that the prepared statement will be retained for a long time and
4479
** probably reused many times.)^ ^Without this flag, [sqlite3_prepare_v3()]
4480
** and [sqlite3_prepare16_v3()] assume that the prepared statement will
4481
** be used just once or at most a few times and then destroyed using
4482
** [sqlite3_finalize()] relatively soon. The current implementation acts
4483
** on this hint by avoiding the use of [lookaside memory] so as not to
4484
** deplete the limited store of lookaside memory. Future versions of
4485
** SQLite may act on this hint differently.
4486
**
4487
** [[SQLITE_PREPARE_NORMALIZE]] <dt>SQLITE_PREPARE_NORMALIZE</dt>
4488
** <dd>The SQLITE_PREPARE_NORMALIZE flag is a no-op. This flag used
4489
** to be required for any prepared statement that wanted to use the
4490
** [sqlite3_normalized_sql()] interface.  However, the
4491
** [sqlite3_normalized_sql()] interface is now available to all
4492
** prepared statements, regardless of whether or not they use this
4493
** flag.
4494
**
4495
** [[SQLITE_PREPARE_NO_VTAB]] <dt>SQLITE_PREPARE_NO_VTAB</dt>
4496
** <dd>The SQLITE_PREPARE_NO_VTAB flag causes the SQL compiler
4497
** to return an error (error code SQLITE_ERROR) if the statement uses
4498
** any virtual tables.
4499
**
4500
** [[SQLITE_PREPARE_DONT_LOG]] <dt>SQLITE_PREPARE_DONT_LOG</dt>
4501
** <dd>The SQLITE_PREPARE_DONT_LOG flag prevents SQL compiler
4502
** errors from being sent to the error log defined by
4503
** [SQLITE_CONFIG_LOG].  This can be used, for example, to do test
4504
** compiles to see if some SQL syntax is well-formed, without generating
4505
** messages on the global error log when it is not.  If the test compile
4506
** fails, the sqlite3_prepare_v3() call returns the same error indications
4507
** with or without this flag; it just omits the call to [sqlite3_log()] that
4508
** logs the error.
4509
**
4510
** [[SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL]] <dt>SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL</dt>
4511
** <dd>The SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL flag causes the SQL compiler to enforce
4512
** security constraints that would otherwise only be enforced when parsing
4513
** the database schema.  In other words, the SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL flag
4514
** causes the SQL compiler to treat the SQL statement being prepared as if
4515
** it had come from an attacker.  When SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL is used and
4516
** [SQLITE_DBCONFIG_TRUSTED_SCHEMA] is off, SQL functions may only be called
4517
** if they are tagged with [SQLITE_INNOCUOUS] and virtual tables may only
4518
** be used if they are tagged with [SQLITE_VTAB_INNOCUOUS].  Best practice
4519
** is to use the SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL option when preparing any SQL that
4520
** is derived from parts of the database schema. In particular, virtual
4521
** table implementations that run SQL statements that are derived from
4522
** arguments to their CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE statement should always use
4523
** [sqlite3_prepare_v3()] and set the SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL flag to
4524
** prevent bypass of the [SQLITE_DBCONFIG_TRUSTED_SCHEMA] security checks.
4525
** </dl>
4526
*/
4527
#define SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT              0x01
4528
#define SQLITE_PREPARE_NORMALIZE               0x02
4529
#define SQLITE_PREPARE_NO_VTAB                 0x04
4530
#define SQLITE_PREPARE_DONT_LOG                0x10
4531
#define SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL                0x20

/*
4534
** CAPI3REF: Compiling An SQL Statement
4535
** KEYWORDS: {SQL statement compiler}
4536
** METHOD: sqlite3
4537
** CONSTRUCTOR: sqlite3_stmt
4538
**
4539
** To execute an SQL statement, it must first be compiled into a byte-code
4540
** program using one of these routines.  Or, in other words, these routines
4541
** are constructors for the [prepared statement] object.
4542
**
4543
** The preferred routine to use is [sqlite3_prepare_v2()].  The
4544
** [sqlite3_prepare()] interface is legacy and should be avoided.
4545
** [sqlite3_prepare_v3()] has an extra
4546
** [SQLITE_PREPARE_FROM_DDL|"prepFlags" option] that is sometimes
4547
** needed for special purpose or to pass along security restrictions.
4548
**
4549
** The use of the UTF-8 interfaces is preferred, as SQLite currently
4550
** does all parsing using UTF-8.  The UTF-16 interfaces are provided
4551
** as a convenience.  The UTF-16 interfaces work by converting the
4552
** input text into UTF-8, then invoking the corresponding UTF-8 interface.
4553
**
4554
** The first argument, "db", is a [database connection] obtained from a
4555
** prior successful call to [sqlite3_open()], [sqlite3_open_v2()] or
4556
** [sqlite3_open16()].  The database connection must not have been closed.
4557
**
4558
** The second argument, "zSql", is the statement to be compiled, encoded
4559
** as either UTF-8 or UTF-16.  The sqlite3_prepare(), sqlite3_prepare_v2(),
4560
** and sqlite3_prepare_v3()
4561
** interfaces use UTF-8, and sqlite3_prepare16(), sqlite3_prepare16_v2(),
4562
** and sqlite3_prepare16_v3() use UTF-16.
4563
**
4564
** ^If the nByte argument is negative, then zSql is read up to the
4565
** first zero terminator. ^If nByte is positive, then it is the maximum
4566
** number of bytes read from zSql.  When nByte is positive, zSql is read
4567
** up to the first zero terminator or until the nByte bytes have been read,
4568
** whichever comes first.  ^If nByte is zero, then no prepared
4569
** statement is generated.
4570
** If the caller knows that the supplied string is nul-terminated, then
4571
** there is a small performance advantage to passing an nByte parameter that
4572
** is the number of bytes in the input string <i>including</i>
4573
** the nul-terminator.
4574
** Note that nByte measures the length of the input in bytes, not
4575
** characters, even for the UTF-16 interfaces.
4576
** For the sqlite3_prepare16() and sqlite3_prepare16_v2() interfaces,
4577
** the nByte value must be even or undefined behavior can result.
4578
**
4579
** ^If pzTail is not NULL then *pzTail is made to point to the first byte
4580
** past the end of the first SQL statement in zSql.  These routines only
4581
** compile the first statement in zSql, so *pzTail is left pointing to
4582
** what remains uncompiled.
4583
**
4584
** ^*ppStmt is left pointing to a compiled [prepared statement] that can be
4585
** executed using [sqlite3_step()].  ^If there is an error, *ppStmt is set
4586
** to NULL.  ^If the input text contains no SQL (if the input is an empty
4587
** string or a comment) then *ppStmt is set to NULL.
4588
** The calling procedure is responsible for deleting the compiled
4589
** SQL statement using [sqlite3_finalize()] after it has finished with it.
4590
** ppStmt may not be NULL.
4591
**
4592
** ^On success, the sqlite3_prepare() family of routines return [SQLITE_OK];
4593
** otherwise an [error code] is returned.
4594
**
4595
** The sqlite3_prepare_v2(), sqlite3_prepare_v3(), sqlite3_prepare16_v2(),
4596
** and sqlite3_prepare16_v3() interfaces are recommended for all new programs.
4597
** The older interfaces (sqlite3_prepare() and sqlite3_prepare16())
4598
** are retained for backwards compatibility, but their use is discouraged.
4599
** ^In the "vX" interfaces, the prepared statement
4600
** that is returned (the [sqlite3_stmt] object) contains a copy of the
4601
** original SQL text. This causes the [sqlite3_step()] interface to
4602
** behave differently in three ways:
4603
**
4604
** <ol>
4605
** <li>
4606
** ^If the database schema changes, instead of returning [SQLITE_SCHEMA] as it
4607
** always used to do, [sqlite3_step()] will automatically recompile the SQL
4608
** statement and try to run it again. As many as [SQLITE_MAX_SCHEMA_RETRY]
4609
** retries will occur before sqlite3_step() gives up and returns an error.
4610
** </li>
4611
**
4612
** <li>
4613
** ^When an error occurs, [sqlite3_step()] will return one of the detailed
4614
** [error codes] or [extended error codes].  ^The legacy behavior was that
4615
** [sqlite3_step()] would only return a generic [SQLITE_ERROR] result code
4616
** and the application would have to make a second call to [sqlite3_reset()]
4617
** in order to find the underlying cause of the problem. With the "v2" prepare
4618
** interfaces, the underlying reason for the error is returned immediately.
4619
** </li>
4620
**
4621
** <li>
4622
** ^If the specific value bound to a [parameter | host parameter] in the
4623
** WHERE clause might influence the choice of query plan for a statement,
4624
** then the statement will be automatically recompiled, as if there had been
4625
** a schema change, on the first [sqlite3_step()] call following any change
4626
** to the [sqlite3_bind_text | bindings] of that [parameter].
4627
** ^The specific value of a WHERE-clause [parameter] might influence the
4628
** choice of query plan if the parameter is the left-hand side of a [LIKE]
4629
** or [GLOB] operator or if the parameter is compared to an indexed column
4630
** and the [SQLITE_ENABLE_STAT4] compile-time option is enabled.
4631
** </li>
4632
** </ol>
4633
**
4634
** <p>^sqlite3_prepare_v3() differs from sqlite3_prepare_v2() only in having
4635
** the extra prepFlags parameter, which is a bit array consisting of zero or
4636
** more of the [SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT|SQLITE_PREPARE_*] flags.  ^The
4637
** sqlite3_prepare_v2() interface works exactly the same as
4638
** sqlite3_prepare_v3() with a zero prepFlags parameter.
4639
*/
4640
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_prepare(
4641
  sqlite3 *db,            /* Database handle */
4642
  const char *zSql,       /* SQL statement, UTF-8 encoded */
4643
  int nByte,              /* Maximum length of zSql in bytes. */
4644
  sqlite3_stmt **ppStmt,  /* OUT: Statement handle */
4645
  const char **pzTail     /* OUT: Pointer to unused portion of zSql */
4646
);
4647
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_prepare_v2(
4648
  sqlite3 *db,            /* Database handle */
4649
  const char *zSql,       /* SQL statement, UTF-8 encoded */
4650
  int nByte,              /* Maximum length of zSql in bytes. */
4651
  sqlite3_stmt **ppStmt,  /* OUT: Statement handle */
4652
  const char **pzTail     /* OUT: Pointer to unused portion of zSql */
4653
);
4654
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_prepare_v3(
4655
  sqlite3 *db,            /* Database handle */
4656
  const char *zSql,       /* SQL statement, UTF-8 encoded */
4657
  int nByte,              /* Maximum length of zSql in bytes. */
4658
  unsigned int prepFlags, /* Zero or more SQLITE_PREPARE_ flags */
4659
  sqlite3_stmt **ppStmt,  /* OUT: Statement handle */
4660
  const char **pzTail     /* OUT: Pointer to unused portion of zSql */
4661
);
4662
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_prepare16(
4663
  sqlite3 *db,            /* Database handle */
4664
  const void *zSql,       /* SQL statement, UTF-16 encoded */
4665
  int nByte,              /* Maximum length of zSql in bytes. */
4666
  sqlite3_stmt **ppStmt,  /* OUT: Statement handle */
4667
  const void **pzTail     /* OUT: Pointer to unused portion of zSql */
4668

4670

4673
  sqlite3_stmt **ppStmt,  /* OUT: Statement handle */
4674
  const void **pzTail     /* OUT: Pointer to unused portion of zSql */
4675

/*
4686
** CAPI3REF: Retrieving Statement SQL
4687
** METHOD: sqlite3_stmt
4688
**
4689
** ^The sqlite3_sql(P) interface returns a pointer to a copy of the UTF-8
4690
** SQL text used to create [prepared statement] P if P was
4691
** created by [sqlite3_prepare_v2()], [sqlite3_prepare_v3()],
4692
** [sqlite3_prepare16_v2()], or [sqlite3_prepare16_v3()].
4693
** ^The sqlite3_expanded_sql(P) interface returns a pointer to a UTF-8
4694
** string containing the SQL text of prepared statement P with
4695
** [bound parameters] expanded.
4696
** ^The sqlite3_normalized_sql(P) interface returns a pointer to a UTF-8
4697
** string containing the normalized SQL text of prepared statement P.  The
4698
** semantics used to normalize a SQL statement are unspecified and subject
4699
** to change.  At a minimum, literal values will be replaced with suitable
4700
** placeholders.
4701
**
4702
** ^(For example, if a prepared statement is created using the SQL
4703
** text "SELECT $abc,:xyz" and if parameter $abc is bound to integer 2345
4704
** and parameter :xyz is unbound, then sqlite3_sql() will return
4705
** the original string, "SELECT $abc,:xyz" but sqlite3_expanded_sql()
4706
** will return "SELECT 2345,NULL".)^
4707
**
4708
** ^The sqlite3_expanded_sql() interface returns NULL if insufficient memory
4709
** is available to hold the result, or if the result would exceed the
4710
** maximum string length determined by the [SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH].
4711
**
4712
** ^The [SQLITE_TRACE_SIZE_LIMIT] compile-time option limits the size of
4713
** bound parameter expansions.  ^The [SQLITE_OMIT_TRACE] compile-time
4714
** option causes sqlite3_expanded_sql() to always return NULL.
4715
**
4716
** ^The strings returned by sqlite3_sql(P) and sqlite3_normalized_sql(P)
4717
** are managed by SQLite and are automatically freed when the prepared
4718
** statement is finalized.
4719
** ^The string returned by sqlite3_expanded_sql(P), on the other hand,
4720
** is obtained from [sqlite3_malloc()] and must be freed by the application
4721
** by passing it to [sqlite3_free()].
4722
**
4723
** ^The sqlite3_normalized_sql() interface is only available if
4724
** the [SQLITE_ENABLE_NORMALIZE] compile-time option is defined.
4725
*/
4726
SQLITE_API const char *sqlite3_sql(sqlite3_stmt *pStmt);

SQLITE_API char *sqlite3_expanded_sql(sqlite3_stmt *pStmt);

4729

/*
4733
** CAPI3REF: Determine If An SQL Statement Writes The Database
4734
** METHOD: sqlite3_stmt
4735
**
4736
** ^The sqlite3_stmt_readonly(X) interface returns true (non-zero) if
4737
** and only if the [prepared statement] X makes no direct changes to
4738
** the content of the database file.
4739
**
4740
** Note that [application-defined SQL functions] or
4741
** [virtual tables] might change the database indirectly as a side effect.
4742
** ^(For example, if an application defines a function "eval()" that
4743
** calls [sqlite3_exec()], then the following SQL statement would
4744
** change the database file through side-effects:
4745
**
4746
** <blockquote><pre>
4747
**    SELECT eval('DELETE FROM t1') FROM t2;
4748
** </pre></blockquote>
4749
**
4750
** But because the [SELECT] statement does not change the database file
4751
** directly, sqlite3_stmt_readonly() would still return true.)^
4752
**
4753
** ^Transaction control statements such as [BEGIN], [COMMIT], [ROLLBACK],
4754
** [SAVEPOINT], and [RELEASE] cause sqlite3_stmt_readonly() to return true,
4755
** since the statements themselves do not actually modify the database but
4756
** rather they control the timing of when other statements modify the
4757
** database.  ^The [ATTACH] and [DETACH] statements also cause
4758
** sqlite3_stmt_readonly() to return true since, while those statements
4759
** change the configuration of a database connection, they do not make
4760
** changes to the content of the database files on disk.
4761
** ^The sqlite3_stmt_readonly() interface returns true for [BEGIN] since
4762
** [BEGIN] merely sets internal flags, but the [BEGIN|BEGIN IMMEDIATE] and
4763
** [BEGIN|BEGIN EXCLUSIVE] commands do touch the database and so
4764
** sqlite3_stmt_readonly() returns false for those commands.
4765
**
4766
** ^This routine returns false if there is any possibility that the
4767
** statement might change the database file.  ^A false return does
4768
** not guarantee that the statement will change the database file.
4769
** ^For example, an UPDATE statement might have a WHERE clause that
4770
** makes it a no-op, but the sqlite3_stmt_readonly() result would still
4771
** be false.  ^Similarly, a CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statement is a
4772
** read-only no-op if the table already exists, but
4773
** sqlite3_stmt_readonly() still returns false for such a statement.
4774
**
4775
** ^If prepared statement X is an [EXPLAIN] or [EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN]
4776
** statement, then sqlite3_stmt_readonly(X) returns the same value as
4777
** if the EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN prefix were omitted.
4778
*/
4779
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_stmt_readonly(sqlite3_stmt *pStmt);
4780
4781
/*
4782
** CAPI3REF: Query The EXPLAIN Setting For A Prepared Statement
4783
** METHOD: sqlite3_stmt
4784
**
4785
** ^The sqlite3_stmt_isexplain(S) interface returns 1 if the
4786
** prepared statement S is an EXPLAIN statement, or 2 if the
4787
** statement S is an EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
4788
** ^The sqlite3_stmt_isexplain(S) interface returns 0 if S is
4789
** an ordinary statement or a NULL pointer.
4790
*/
4791
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_stmt_isexplain(sqlite3_stmt *pStmt);
4792
4793
/*
4794
** CAPI3REF: Change The EXPLAIN Setting For A Prepared Statement
4795
** METHOD: sqlite3_stmt
4796
**
4797
** The sqlite3_stmt_explain(S,E) interface changes the EXPLAIN
4798
** setting for [prepared statement] S.  If E is zero, then S becomes
4799
** a normal prepared statement.  If E is 1, then S behaves as if
4800
** its SQL text began with "[EXPLAIN]".  If E is 2, then S behaves as if
4801
** its SQL text began with "[EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN]".
4802
**
4803
** Calling sqlite3_stmt_explain(S,E) might cause S to be reprepared.
4804
** SQLite tries to avoid a reprepare, but a reprepare might be necessary
4805
** on the first transition into EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN mode.
4806
**
4807
** Because of the potential need to reprepare, a call to
4808
** sqlite3_stmt_explain(S,E) will fail with SQLITE_ERROR if S cannot be
4809
** reprepared because it was created using [sqlite3_prepare()] instead of
4810
** the newer [sqlite3_prepare_v2()] or [sqlite3_prepare_v3()] interfaces and
4811
** hence has no saved SQL text with which to reprepare.
4812
**
4813
** Changing the explain setting for a prepared statement does not change
4814
** the original SQL text for the statement.  Hence, if the SQL text originally
4815
** began with EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, but sqlite3_stmt_explain(S,0)
4816
** is called to convert the statement into an ordinary statement, the EXPLAIN
4817
** or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN keywords will still appear in the sqlite3_sql(S)
4818
** output, even though the statement now acts like a normal SQL statement.
4819
**
4820
** This routine returns SQLITE_OK if the explain mode is successfully
4821
** changed, or an error code if the explain mode could not be changed.
4822
** The explain mode cannot be changed while a statement is active.
4823
** Hence, it is good practice to call [sqlite3_reset(S)]
4824
** immediately prior to calling sqlite3_stmt_explain(S,E).
4825
*/
4826
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_stmt_explain(sqlite3_stmt *pStmt, int eMode);
4827

/*
4829
** CAPI3REF: Determine If A Prepared Statement Has Been Reset
4830
** METHOD: sqlite3_stmt
4831
**
4832
** ^The sqlite3_stmt_busy(S) interface returns true (non-zero) if the
4833
** [prepared statement] S has been stepped at least once using
4834
** [sqlite3_step(S)] but has neither run to completion (returned
4835
** [SQLITE_DONE] from [sqlite3_step(S)]) nor
4836
** been reset using [sqlite3_reset(S)].  ^The sqlite3_stmt_busy(S)
4837
** interface returns false if S is a NULL pointer.  If S is not a
4838
** NULL pointer and is not a pointer to a valid [prepared statement]
4839
** object, then the behavior is undefined and probably undesirable.
4840
**
4841
** This interface can be used in combination [sqlite3_next_stmt()]
4842
** to locate all prepared statements associated with a database
4843
** connection that are in need of being reset.  This can be used,
4844
** for example, in diagnostic routines to search for prepared
4845
** statements that are holding a transaction open.
4846
*/
4847
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_stmt_busy(sqlite3_stmt*);
