7703
/*
7704
** CAPI3REF: Reset Automatic Extension Loading
7705
**
7706
** ^This interface disables all automatic extensions previously
7707
** registered using [sqlite3_auto_extension()].
7708
*/
7709
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_reset_auto_extension(void);
7710
7711
/*
7712
** Structures used by the virtual table interface
7713
*/
7714
typedef struct sqlite3_vtab sqlite3_vtab;
7715
typedef struct sqlite3_index_info sqlite3_index_info;
7716
typedef struct sqlite3_vtab_cursor sqlite3_vtab_cursor;
7717
typedef struct sqlite3_module sqlite3_module;
7718
7719
/*
7720
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Object
7721
** KEYWORDS: sqlite3_module {virtual table module}
7722
**
7723
** This structure, sometimes called a "virtual table module",
7724
** defines the implementation of a [virtual table].
7725
** This structure consists mostly of methods for the module.
7726
**
7727
** ^A virtual table module is created by filling in a persistent
7728
** instance of this structure and passing a pointer to that instance
7729
** to [sqlite3_create_module()] or [sqlite3_create_module_v2()].
7730
** ^The registration remains valid until it is replaced by a different
7731
** module or until the [database connection] closes.  The content
7732
** of this structure must not change while it is registered with
7733
** any database connection.
7734
*/
7735
struct sqlite3_module {
7736
  int iVersion;
7737
  int (*xCreate)(sqlite3*, void *pAux,
7738
               int argc, const char *const*argv,
7739
               sqlite3_vtab **ppVTab, char**);
7740
  int (*xConnect)(sqlite3*, void *pAux,
7741
               int argc, const char *const*argv,
7742
               sqlite3_vtab **ppVTab, char**);
7743
  int (*xBestIndex)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, sqlite3_index_info*);
7744
  int (*xDisconnect)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7745
  int (*xDestroy)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7746
  int (*xOpen)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, sqlite3_vtab_cursor **ppCursor);
7747
  int (*xClose)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*);
7748
  int (*xFilter)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*, int idxNum, const char *idxStr,
7749
                int argc, sqlite3_value **argv);
7750
  int (*xNext)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*);
7751
  int (*xEof)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*);
7752
  int (*xColumn)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*, sqlite3_context*, int);
7753
  int (*xRowid)(sqlite3_vtab_cursor*, sqlite3_int64 *pRowid);
7754
  int (*xUpdate)(sqlite3_vtab *, int, sqlite3_value **, sqlite3_int64 *);
7755
  int (*xBegin)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7756
  int (*xSync)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7757
  int (*xCommit)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7758
  int (*xRollback)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab);
7759
  int (*xFindFunction)(sqlite3_vtab *pVtab, int nArg, const char *zName,
7760
                       void (**pxFunc)(sqlite3_context*,int,sqlite3_value**),
7761
                       void **ppArg);
7762
  int (*xRename)(sqlite3_vtab *pVtab, const char *zNew);
7763
  /* The methods above are in version 1 of the sqlite_module object. Those
7764
  ** below are for version 2 and greater. */
7765
  int (*xSavepoint)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, int);
7766
  int (*xRelease)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, int);
7767
  int (*xRollbackTo)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, int);
7768
  /* The methods above are in versions 1 and 2 of the sqlite_module object.
7769
  ** Those below are for version 3 and greater. */
7770
  int (*xShadowName)(const char*);
7771
  /* The methods above are in versions 1 through 3 of the sqlite_module object.
7772
  ** Those below are for version 4 and greater. */
7773
  int (*xIntegrity)(sqlite3_vtab *pVTab, const char *zSchema,
7774
                    const char *zTabName, int mFlags, char **pzErr);
7775
};
7776
7777
/*
7778
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Indexing Information
7779
** KEYWORDS: sqlite3_index_info
7780
**
7781
** The sqlite3_index_info structure and its substructures is used as part
7782
** of the [virtual table] interface to
7783
** pass information into and receive the reply from the [xBestIndex]
7784
** method of a [virtual table module].  The fields under **Inputs** are the
7785
** inputs to xBestIndex and are read-only.  xBestIndex inserts its
7786
** results into the **Outputs** fields.
7787
**
7788
** ^(The aConstraint[] array records WHERE clause constraints of the form:
7789
**
7790
** <blockquote>column OP expr</blockquote>
7791
**
7792
** where OP is =, &lt;, &lt;=, &gt;, or &gt;=.)^  ^(The particular operator is
7793
** stored in aConstraint[].op using one of the
7794
** [SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_EQ | SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ values].)^
7795
** ^(The index of the column is stored in
7796
** aConstraint[].iColumn.)^  ^(aConstraint[].usable is TRUE if the
7797
** expr on the right-hand side can be evaluated (and thus the constraint
7798
** is usable) and false if it cannot.)^
7799
**
7800
** ^The optimizer automatically inverts terms of the form "expr OP column"
7801
** and makes other simplifications to the WHERE clause in an attempt to
7802
** get as many WHERE clause terms into the form shown above as possible.
7803
** ^The aConstraint[] array only reports WHERE clause terms that are
7804
** relevant to the particular virtual table being queried.
7805
**
7806
** ^Information about the ORDER BY clause is stored in aOrderBy[].
7807
** ^Each term of aOrderBy records a column of the ORDER BY clause.
7808
**
7809
** The colUsed field indicates which columns of the virtual table may be
7810
** required by the current scan. Virtual table columns are numbered from
7811
** zero in the order in which they appear within the CREATE TABLE statement
7812
** passed to sqlite3_declare_vtab(). For the first 63 columns (columns 0-62),
7813
** the corresponding bit is set within the colUsed mask if the column may be
7814
** required by SQLite. If the table has at least 64 columns and any column
7815
** to the right of the first 63 is required, then bit 63 of colUsed is also
7816
** set. In other words, column iCol may be required if the expression
7817
** (colUsed & ((sqlite3_uint64)1 << (iCol>=63 ? 63 : iCol))) evaluates to
7818
** non-zero.
7819
**
7820
** The [xBestIndex] method must fill aConstraintUsage[] with information
7821
** about what parameters to pass to xFilter.  ^If argvIndex>0 then
7822
** the right-hand side of the corresponding aConstraint[] is evaluated
7823
** and becomes the argvIndex-th entry in argv.  ^(If aConstraintUsage[].omit
7824
** is true, then the constraint is assumed to be fully handled by the
7825
** virtual table and might not be checked again by the byte code.)^ ^(The
7826
** aConstraintUsage[].omit flag is an optimization hint. When the omit flag
7827
** is left in its default setting of false, the constraint will always be
7828
** checked separately in byte code.  If the omit flag is changed to true, then
7829
** the constraint may or may not be checked in byte code.  In other words,
7830
** when the omit flag is true there is no guarantee that the constraint will
7831
** not be checked again using byte code.)^
7832
**
7833
** ^The idxNum and idxStr values are recorded and passed into the
7834
** [xFilter] method.
7835
** ^[sqlite3_free()] is used to free idxStr if and only if
7836
** needToFreeIdxStr is true.
7837
**
7838
** ^The orderByConsumed means that output from [xFilter]/[xNext] will occur in
7839
** the correct order to satisfy the ORDER BY clause so that no separate
7840
** sorting step is required.
7841
**
7842
** ^The estimatedCost value is an estimate of the cost of a particular
7843
** strategy. A cost of N indicates that the cost of the strategy is similar
7844
** to a linear scan of an SQLite table with N rows. A cost of log(N)
7845
** indicates that the expense of the operation is similar to that of a
7846
** binary search on a unique indexed field of an SQLite table with N rows.
7847
**
7848
** ^The estimatedRows value is an estimate of the number of rows that
7849
** will be returned by the strategy.
7850
**
7851
** The xBestIndex method may optionally populate the idxFlags field with a
7852
** mask of SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_* flags. One such flag is
7853
** [SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_HEX], which if set causes the [EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN]
7854
** output to show the idxNum as hex instead of as decimal.  Another flag is
7855
** SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_UNIQUE, which if set indicates that the query plan will
7856
** return at most one row.
7857
**
7858
** Additionally, if xBestIndex sets the SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_UNIQUE flag, then
7859
** SQLite also assumes that if a call to the xUpdate() method is made as
7860
** part of the same statement to delete or update a virtual table row and the
7861
** implementation returns SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, then there is no need to rollback
7862
** any database changes. In other words, if the xUpdate() returns
7863
** SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, the database contents must be exactly as they were
7864
** before xUpdate was called. By contrast, if SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_UNIQUE is not
7865
** set and xUpdate returns SQLITE_CONSTRAINT, any database changes made by
7866
** the xUpdate method are automatically rolled back by SQLite.
7867
**
7868
** IMPORTANT: The estimatedRows field was added to the sqlite3_index_info
7869
** structure for SQLite [version 3.8.2] ([dateof:3.8.2]).
7870
** If a virtual table extension is
7871
** used with an SQLite version earlier than 3.8.2, the results of attempting
7872
** to read or write the estimatedRows field are undefined (but are likely
7873
** to include crashing the application). The estimatedRows field should
7874
** therefore only be used if [sqlite3_libversion_number()] returns a
7875
** value greater than or equal to 3008002. Similarly, the idxFlags field
7876
** was added for [version 3.9.0] ([dateof:3.9.0]).
7877
** It may therefore only be used if
7878
** sqlite3_libversion_number() returns a value greater than or equal to
7879
** 3009000.
7880
*/
7881
struct sqlite3_index_info {
7882
  /* Inputs */
7883
  int nConstraint;           /* Number of entries in aConstraint */
7884
  struct sqlite3_index_constraint {
7885
     int iColumn;              /* Column constrained.  -1 for ROWID */
7886
     unsigned char op;         /* Constraint operator */
7887
     unsigned char usable;     /* True if this constraint is usable */
7888
     int iTermOffset;          /* Used internally - xBestIndex should ignore */
7889
  } *aConstraint;            /* Table of WHERE clause constraints */
7890
  int nOrderBy;              /* Number of terms in the ORDER BY clause */
7891
  struct sqlite3_index_orderby {
7892
     int iColumn;              /* Column number */
7893
     unsigned char desc;       /* True for DESC.  False for ASC. */
7894
  } *aOrderBy;               /* The ORDER BY clause */
7895
  /* Outputs */
7896
  struct sqlite3_index_constraint_usage {
7897
    int argvIndex;           /* if >0, constraint is part of argv to xFilter */
7898
    unsigned char omit;      /* Do not code a test for this constraint */
7899
  } *aConstraintUsage;
7900
  int idxNum;                /* Number used to identify the index */
7901
  char *idxStr;              /* String, possibly obtained from sqlite3_malloc */
7902
  int needToFreeIdxStr;      /* Free idxStr using sqlite3_free() if true */
7903
  int orderByConsumed;       /* True if output is already ordered */
7904
  double estimatedCost;           /* Estimated cost of using this index */
7905
  /* Fields below are only available in SQLite 3.8.2 and later */
7906
  sqlite3_int64 estimatedRows;    /* Estimated number of rows returned */
7907
  /* Fields below are only available in SQLite 3.9.0 and later */
7908
  int idxFlags;              /* Mask of SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_* flags */
7909
  /* Fields below are only available in SQLite 3.10.0 and later */
7910
  sqlite3_uint64 colUsed;    /* Input: Mask of columns used by statement */
7911
};
7912
7913
/*
7914
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Scan Flags
7915
**
7916
** Virtual table implementations are allowed to set the
7917
** [sqlite3_index_info].idxFlags field to some combination of
7918
** these bits.
7919
*/
7920
#define SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_UNIQUE 0x00000001 /* Scan visits at most 1 row */
7921
#define SQLITE_INDEX_SCAN_HEX    0x00000002 /* Display idxNum as hex */
7922
                                            /* in EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN */
7923
7924
/*
7925
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Constraint Operator Codes
7926
**
7927
** These macros define the allowed values for the
7928
** [sqlite3_index_info].aConstraint[].op field.  Each value represents
7929
** an operator that is part of a constraint term in the WHERE clause of
7930
** a query that uses a [virtual table].
7931
**
7932
** ^The left-hand operand of the operator is given by the corresponding
7933
** aConstraint[].iColumn field.  ^An iColumn of -1 indicates the left-hand
7934
** operand is the rowid.
7935
** The SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_LIMIT and SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_OFFSET
7936
** operators have no left-hand operand, and so for those operators the
7937
** corresponding aConstraint[].iColumn is meaningless and should not be
7938
** used.
7939
**
7940
** All operator values from SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_FUNCTION through
7941
** value 255 are reserved to represent functions that are overloaded
7942
** by the [xFindFunction|xFindFunction method] of the virtual table
7943
** implementation.
7944
**
7945
** The right-hand operands for each constraint might be accessible using
7946
** the [sqlite3_vtab_rhs_value()] interface.  Usually the right-hand
7947
** operand is only available if it appears as a single constant literal
7948
** in the input SQL.  If the right-hand operand is another column or an
7949
** expression (even a constant expression) or a parameter, then the
7950
** sqlite3_vtab_rhs_value() probably will not be able to extract it.
7951
** ^The SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ISNULL and
7952
** SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ISNOTNULL operators have no right-hand operand
7953
** and hence calls to sqlite3_vtab_rhs_value() for those operators will
7954
** always return SQLITE_NOTFOUND.
7955
**
7956
** The collating sequence to be used for comparison can be found using
7957
** the [sqlite3_vtab_collation()] interface.  For most real-world virtual
7958
** tables, the collating sequence of constraints does not matter (for example
7959
** because the constraints are numeric) and so the sqlite3_vtab_collation()
7960
** interface is not commonly needed.
7961
*/
7962
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_EQ          2
7963
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_GT          4
7964
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_LE          8
7965
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_LT         16
7966
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_GE         32
7967
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_MATCH      64
7968
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_LIKE       65
7969
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_GLOB       66
7970
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_REGEXP     67
7971
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_NE         68
7972
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ISNOT      69
7973
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ISNOTNULL  70
7974
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_ISNULL     71
7975
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_IS         72
7976
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_LIMIT      73
7977
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_OFFSET     74
7978
#define SQLITE_INDEX_CONSTRAINT_FUNCTION  150
7979
7980
/*
7981
** CAPI3REF: Register A Virtual Table Implementation
7982
** METHOD: sqlite3
7983
**
7984
** ^These routines are used to register a new [virtual table module] name.
7985
** ^Module names must be registered before
7986
** creating a new [virtual table] using the module and before using a
7987
** preexisting [virtual table] for the module.
7988
**
7989
** ^The module name is registered on the [database connection] specified
7990
** by the first parameter.  ^The name of the module is given by the
7991
** second parameter.  ^The third parameter is a pointer to
7992
** the implementation of the [virtual table module].   ^The fourth
7993
** parameter is an arbitrary client data pointer that is passed through
7994
** into the [xCreate] and [xConnect] methods of the virtual table module
7995
** when a new virtual table is being created or reinitialized.
7996
**
7997
** ^The sqlite3_create_module_v2() interface has a fifth parameter which
7998
** is a pointer to a destructor for the pClientData.  ^SQLite will
7999
** invoke the destructor function (if it is not NULL) when SQLite
8000
** no longer needs the pClientData pointer.  ^The destructor will also
8001
** be invoked if the call to sqlite3_create_module_v2() fails.
8002
** ^The sqlite3_create_module()
8003
** interface is equivalent to sqlite3_create_module_v2() with a NULL
8004
** destructor.
8005
**
8006
** ^If the third parameter (the pointer to the sqlite3_module object) is
8007
** NULL then no new module is created and any existing modules with the
8008
** same name are dropped.
8009
**
8010
** See also: [sqlite3_drop_modules()]
8011
*/
8012
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_create_module(
8013
  sqlite3 *db,               /* SQLite connection to register module with */
8014
  const char *zName,         /* Name of the module */
8015
  const sqlite3_module *p,   /* Methods for the module */
8016
  void *pClientData          /* Client data for xCreate/xConnect */
8017
);
8018
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_create_module_v2(
8019
  sqlite3 *db,               /* SQLite connection to register module with */
8020
  const char *zName,         /* Name of the module */
8021
  const sqlite3_module *p,   /* Methods for the module */
8022
  void *pClientData,         /* Client data for xCreate/xConnect */
8023
  void(*xDestroy)(void*)     /* Module destructor function */
8024
);
8025
8026
/*
8027
** CAPI3REF: Remove Unnecessary Virtual Table Implementations
8028
** METHOD: sqlite3
8029
**
8030
** ^The sqlite3_drop_modules(D,L) interface removes all virtual
8031
** table modules from database connection D except those named on list L.
8032
** The L parameter must be either NULL or a pointer to an array of pointers
8033
** to strings where the array is terminated by a single NULL pointer.
8034
** ^If the L parameter is NULL, then all virtual table modules are removed.
8035
**
8036
** See also: [sqlite3_create_module()]
8037
*/
8038
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_drop_modules(
8039
  sqlite3 *db,                /* Remove modules from this connection */
8040
  const char **azKeep         /* Except, do not remove the ones named here */
8041
);
8042
8043
/*
8044
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Instance Object
8045
** KEYWORDS: sqlite3_vtab
8046
**
8047
** Every [virtual table module] implementation uses a subclass
8048
** of this object to describe a particular instance
8049
** of the [virtual table].  Each subclass will
8050
** be tailored to the specific needs of the module implementation.
8051
** The purpose of this superclass is to define certain fields that are
8052
** common to all module implementations.
8053
**
8054
** ^Virtual tables methods can set an error message by assigning a
8055
** string obtained from [sqlite3_mprintf()] to zErrMsg.  The method should
8056
** take care that any prior string is freed by a call to [sqlite3_free()]
8057
** prior to assigning a new string to zErrMsg.  ^After the error message
8058
** is delivered up to the client application, the string will be automatically
8059
** freed by sqlite3_free() and the zErrMsg field will be zeroed.
8060
*/
8061
struct sqlite3_vtab {
8062
  const sqlite3_module *pModule;  /* The module for this virtual table */
8063
  int nRef;                       /* Number of open cursors */
8064
  char *zErrMsg;                  /* Error message from sqlite3_mprintf() */
8065
  /* Virtual table implementations will typically add additional fields */
8066
};
8067
8068
/*
8069
** CAPI3REF: Virtual Table Cursor Object
8070
** KEYWORDS: sqlite3_vtab_cursor {virtual table cursor}
8071
**
8072
** Every [virtual table module] implementation uses a subclass of the
8073
** following structure to describe cursors that point into the
8074
** [virtual table] and are used
8075
** to loop through the virtual table.  Cursors are created using the
8076
** [sqlite3_module.xOpen | xOpen] method of the module and are destroyed
8077
** by the [sqlite3_module.xClose | xClose] method.  Cursors are used
8078
** by the [xFilter], [xNext], [xEof], [xColumn], and [xRowid] methods
8079
** of the module.  Each module implementation will define
8080
** the content of a cursor structure to suit its own needs.
8081
**
8082
** This superclass exists in order to define fields of the cursor that
8083
** are common to all implementations.
8084
*/
8085
struct sqlite3_vtab_cursor {
8086
  sqlite3_vtab *pVtab;      /* Virtual table of this cursor */
8087
  /* Virtual table implementations will typically add additional fields */
8088
};
8089
8090
/*
8091
** CAPI3REF: Declare The Schema Of A Virtual Table
8092
**
8093
** ^The [xCreate] and [xConnect] methods of a
8094
** [virtual table module] call this interface
8095
** to declare the format (the names and datatypes of the columns) of
8096
** the virtual tables they implement.
8097
*/
8098
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_declare_vtab(sqlite3*, const char *zSQL);
8099
8100
/*
8101
** CAPI3REF: Overload A Function For A Virtual Table
8102
** METHOD: sqlite3
8103
**
8104
** ^(Virtual tables can provide alternative implementations of functions
8105
** using the [xFindFunction] method of the [virtual table module].
8106
** But global versions of those functions
8107
** must exist in order to be overloaded.)^
8108
**
8109
** ^(This API makes sure a global version of a function with a particular
8110
** name and number of parameters exists.  If no such function exists
8111
** before this API is called, a new function is created.)^  ^The implementation
8112
** of the new function always causes an exception to be thrown.  So
8113
** the new function is not good for anything by itself.  Its only
8114
** purpose is to be a placeholder function that can be overloaded
8115
** by a [virtual table].
8116
*/
8117
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_overload_function(sqlite3*, const char *zFuncName, int nArg);
8118
8119
/*
8120
** CAPI3REF: A Handle To An Open BLOB
8121
** KEYWORDS: {BLOB handle} {BLOB handles}
8122
**
8123
** An instance of this object represents an open BLOB on which
8124
** [sqlite3_blob_open | incremental BLOB I/O] can be performed.
8125
** ^Objects of this type are created by [sqlite3_blob_open()]
8126
** and destroyed by [sqlite3_blob_close()].
8127
** ^The [sqlite3_blob_read()] and [sqlite3_blob_write()] interfaces
8128
** can be used to read or write small subsections of the BLOB.
8129
** ^The [sqlite3_blob_bytes()] interface returns the size of the BLOB in bytes.
8130
*/
8131
typedef struct sqlite3_blob sqlite3_blob;
8132
8133
/*
8134
** CAPI3REF: Open A BLOB For Incremental I/O
8135
** METHOD: sqlite3
8136
** CONSTRUCTOR: sqlite3_blob
8137
**
8138
** ^(This interfaces opens a [BLOB handle | handle] to the BLOB located
8139
** in row iRow, column zColumn, table zTable in database zDb;
8140
** in other words, the same BLOB that would be selected by:
8141
**
8142
** <pre>
8143
**     SELECT zColumn FROM zDb.zTable WHERE [rowid] = iRow;
8144
** </pre>)^
8145
**
8146
** ^(Parameter zDb is not the filename that contains the database, but
8147
** rather the symbolic name of the database. For attached databases, this is
8148
** the name that appears after the AS keyword in the [ATTACH] statement.
8149
** For the main database file, the database name is "main". For TEMP
8150
** tables, the database name is "temp".)^
8151
**
8152
** ^If the flags parameter is non-zero, then the BLOB is opened for read
8153
** and write access. ^If the flags parameter is zero, the BLOB is opened for
8154
** read-only access.
8155
**
8156
** ^(On success, [SQLITE_OK] is returned and the new [BLOB handle] is stored
8157
** in *ppBlob. Otherwise an [error code] is returned and, unless the error
8158
** code is SQLITE_MISUSE, *ppBlob is set to NULL.)^ ^This means that, provided
8159
** the API is not misused, it is always safe to call [sqlite3_blob_close()]
8160
** on *ppBlob after this function returns.
8161
**
8162
** This function fails with SQLITE_ERROR if any of the following are true:
8163
** <ul>
8164
**   <li> ^(Database zDb does not exist)^,
8165
**   <li> ^(Table zTable does not exist within database zDb)^,
8166
**   <li> ^(Table zTable is a WITHOUT ROWID table)^,
8167
**   <li> ^(Column zColumn does not exist)^,
8168
**   <li> ^(Row iRow is not present in the table)^,
8169
**   <li> ^(The specified column of row iRow contains a value that is not
8170
**         a TEXT or BLOB value)^,
8171
**   <li> ^(Column zColumn is part of an index, PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE
8172
**         constraint and the blob is being opened for read/write access)^,
8173
**   <li> ^([foreign key constraints | Foreign key constraints] are enabled,
8174
**         column zColumn is part of a [child key] definition and the blob is
8175
**         being opened for read/write access)^.
8176
** </ul>
8177
**
8178
** ^Unless it returns SQLITE_MISUSE, this function sets the
8179
** [database connection] error code and message accessible via
8180
** [sqlite3_errcode()] and [sqlite3_errmsg()] and related functions.
8181
**
8182
** A BLOB referenced by sqlite3_blob_open() may be read using the
8183
** [sqlite3_blob_read()] interface and modified by using
8184
** [sqlite3_blob_write()].  The [BLOB handle] can be moved to a
8185
** different row of the same table using the [sqlite3_blob_reopen()]
8186
** interface.  However, the column, table, or database of a [BLOB handle]
8187
** cannot be changed after the [BLOB handle] is opened.
8188
**
8189
** ^(If the row that a BLOB handle points to is modified by an
8190
** [UPDATE], [DELETE], or by [ON CONFLICT] side-effects
8191
** then the BLOB handle is marked as "expired".
8192
** This is true if any column of the row is changed, even a column
8193
** other than the one the BLOB handle is open on.)^
8194
** ^Calls to [sqlite3_blob_read()] and [sqlite3_blob_write()] for
8195
** an expired BLOB handle fail with a return code of [SQLITE_ABORT].
8196
** ^(Changes written into a BLOB prior to the BLOB expiring are not
8197
** rolled back by the expiration of the BLOB.  Such changes will eventually
8198
** commit if the transaction continues to completion.)^
8199
**
8200
** ^Use the [sqlite3_blob_bytes()] interface to determine the size of
8201
** the opened blob.  ^The size of a blob may not be changed by this
8202
** interface.  Use the [UPDATE] SQL command to change the size of a
8203
** blob.
8204
**
8205
** ^The [sqlite3_bind_zeroblob()] and [sqlite3_result_zeroblob()] interfaces
8206
** and the built-in [zeroblob] SQL function may be used to create a
8207
** zero-filled blob to read or write using the incremental-blob interface.
8208
**
8209
** To avoid a resource leak, every open [BLOB handle] should eventually
8210
** be released by a call to [sqlite3_blob_close()].
8211
**
8212
** See also: [sqlite3_blob_close()],
8213
** [sqlite3_blob_reopen()], [sqlite3_blob_read()],
8214
** [sqlite3_blob_bytes()], [sqlite3_blob_write()].
8215
*/
8216
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_open(
8217
  sqlite3*,
8218
  const char *zDb,
8219
  const char *zTable,
8220
  const char *zColumn,
8221
  sqlite3_int64 iRow,
8222
  int flags,
8223
  sqlite3_blob **ppBlob
8224
);
8225
8226
/*
8227
** CAPI3REF: Move a BLOB Handle to a New Row
8228
** METHOD: sqlite3_blob
8229
**
8230
** ^This function is used to move an existing [BLOB handle] so that it points
8231
** to a different row of the same database table. ^The new row is identified
8232
** by the rowid value passed as the second argument. Only the row can be
8233
** changed. ^The database, table and column on which the blob handle is open
8234
** remain the same. Moving an existing [BLOB handle] to a new row is
8235
** faster than closing the existing handle and opening a new one.
8236
**
8237
** ^(The new row must meet the same criteria as for [sqlite3_blob_open()] -
8238
** it must exist and there must be either a blob or text value stored in
8239
** the nominated column.)^ ^If the new row is not present in the table, or if
8240
** it does not contain a blob or text value, or if another error occurs, an
8241
** SQLite error code is returned and the blob handle is considered aborted.
8242
** ^All subsequent calls to [sqlite3_blob_read()], [sqlite3_blob_write()] or
8243
** [sqlite3_blob_reopen()] on an aborted blob handle immediately return
8244
** SQLITE_ABORT. ^Calling [sqlite3_blob_bytes()] on an aborted blob handle
8245
** always returns zero.
8246
**
8247
** ^This function sets the database handle error code and message.
8248
*/
8249
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_reopen(sqlite3_blob *, sqlite3_int64);
8250
8251
/*
8252
** CAPI3REF: Close A BLOB Handle
8253
** DESTRUCTOR: sqlite3_blob
8254
**
8255
** ^This function closes an open [BLOB handle]. ^(The BLOB handle is closed
8256
** unconditionally.  Even if this routine returns an error code, the
8257
** handle is still closed.)^
8258
**
8259
** ^If the blob handle being closed was opened for read-write access, and if
8260
** the database is in auto-commit mode and there are no other open read-write
8261
** blob handles or active write statements, the current transaction is
8262
** committed. ^If an error occurs while committing the transaction, an error
8263
** code is returned and the transaction rolled back.
8264
**
8265
** Calling this function with an argument that is not a NULL pointer or an
8266
** open blob handle results in undefined behavior. ^Calling this routine
8267
** with a null pointer (such as would be returned by a failed call to
8268
** [sqlite3_blob_open()]) is a harmless no-op. ^Otherwise, if this function
8269
** is passed a valid open blob handle, the values returned by the
8270
** sqlite3_errcode() and sqlite3_errmsg() functions are set before returning.
8271
*/
8272
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_close(sqlite3_blob *);
8273
8274
/*
8275
** CAPI3REF: Return The Size Of An Open BLOB
8276
** METHOD: sqlite3_blob
8277
**
8278
** ^Returns the size in bytes of the BLOB accessible via the
8279
** successfully opened [BLOB handle] in its only argument.  ^The
8280
** incremental blob I/O routines can only read or overwrite existing
8281
** blob content; they cannot change the size of a blob.
8282
**
8283
** This routine only works on a [BLOB handle] which has been created
8284
** by a prior successful call to [sqlite3_blob_open()] and which has not
8285
** been closed by [sqlite3_blob_close()].  Passing any other pointer in
8286
** to this routine results in undefined and probably undesirable behavior.
8287
*/
8288
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_bytes(sqlite3_blob *);
8289
8290
/*
8291
** CAPI3REF: Read Data From A BLOB Incrementally
8292
** METHOD: sqlite3_blob
8293
**
8294
** ^(This function is used to read data from an open [BLOB handle] into a
8295
** caller-supplied buffer. N bytes of data are copied into buffer Z
8296
** from the open BLOB, starting at offset iOffset.)^
8297
**
8298
** ^If offset iOffset is less than N bytes from the end of the BLOB,
8299
** [SQLITE_ERROR] is returned and no data is read.  ^If N or iOffset is
8300
** less than zero, [SQLITE_ERROR] is returned and no data is read.
8301
** ^The size of the blob (and hence the maximum value of N+iOffset)
8302
** can be determined using the [sqlite3_blob_bytes()] interface.
8303
**
8304
** ^An attempt to read from an expired [BLOB handle] fails with an
8305
** error code of [SQLITE_ABORT].
8306
**
8307
** ^(On success, sqlite3_blob_read() returns SQLITE_OK.
8308
** Otherwise, an [error code] or an [extended error code] is returned.)^
8309
**
8310
** This routine only works on a [BLOB handle] which has been created
8311
** by a prior successful call to [sqlite3_blob_open()] and which has not
8312
** been closed by [sqlite3_blob_close()].  Passing any other pointer in
8313
** to this routine results in undefined and probably undesirable behavior.
8314
**
8315
** See also: [sqlite3_blob_write()].
8316
*/
8317
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_read(sqlite3_blob *, void *Z, int N, int iOffset);
8318
8319
/*
8320
** CAPI3REF: Write Data Into A BLOB Incrementally
8321
** METHOD: sqlite3_blob
8322
**
8323
** ^(This function is used to write data into an open [BLOB handle] from a
8324
** caller-supplied buffer. N bytes of data are copied from the buffer Z
8325
** into the open BLOB, starting at offset iOffset.)^
8326
**
8327
** ^(On success, sqlite3_blob_write() returns SQLITE_OK.
8328
** Otherwise, an  [error code] or an [extended error code] is returned.)^
8329
** ^Unless SQLITE_MISUSE is returned, this function sets the
8330
** [database connection] error code and message accessible via
8331
** [sqlite3_errcode()] and [sqlite3_errmsg()] and related functions.
8332
**
8333
** ^If the [BLOB handle] passed as the first argument was not opened for
8334
** writing (the flags parameter to [sqlite3_blob_open()] was zero),
8335
** this function returns [SQLITE_READONLY].
8336
**
8337
** This function may only modify the contents of the BLOB; it is
8338
** not possible to increase the size of a BLOB using this API.
8339
** ^If offset iOffset is less than N bytes from the end of the BLOB,
8340
** [SQLITE_ERROR] is returned and no data is written. The size of the
8341
** BLOB (and hence the maximum value of N+iOffset) can be determined
8342
** using the [sqlite3_blob_bytes()] interface. ^If N or iOffset are less
8343
** than zero [SQLITE_ERROR] is returned and no data is written.
8344
**
8345
** ^An attempt to write to an expired [BLOB handle] fails with an
8346
** error code of [SQLITE_ABORT].  ^Writes to the BLOB that occurred
8347
** before the [BLOB handle] expired are not rolled back by the
8348
** expiration of the handle, though of course those changes might
8349
** have been overwritten by the statement that expired the BLOB handle
8350
** or by other independent statements.
8351
**
8352
** This routine only works on a [BLOB handle] which has been created
8353
** by a prior successful call to [sqlite3_blob_open()] and which has not
8354
** been closed by [sqlite3_blob_close()].  Passing any other pointer in
8355
** to this routine results in undefined and probably undesirable behavior.
8356
**
8357
** See also: [sqlite3_blob_read()].
8358
*/
8359
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_blob_write(sqlite3_blob *, const void *z, int n, int iOffset);
8360
8361
/*
8362
** CAPI3REF: Virtual File System Objects
8363
**
8364
** A virtual filesystem (VFS) is an [sqlite3_vfs] object
8365
** that SQLite uses to interact
8366
** with the underlying operating system.  Most SQLite builds come with a
8367
** single default VFS that is appropriate for the host computer.
8368
** New VFSes can be registered and existing VFSes can be unregistered.
8369
** The following interfaces are provided.
8370
**
8371
** ^The sqlite3_vfs_find() interface returns a pointer to a VFS given its name.
8372
** ^Names are case sensitive.
8373
** ^Names are zero-terminated UTF-8 strings.
8374
** ^If there is no match, a NULL pointer is returned.
8375
** ^If zVfsName is NULL then the default VFS is returned.
8376
**
8377
** ^New VFSes are registered with sqlite3_vfs_register().
8378
** ^Each new VFS becomes the default VFS if the makeDflt flag is set.
8379
** ^The same VFS can be registered multiple times without injury.
8380
** ^To make an existing VFS into the default VFS, register it again
8381
** with the makeDflt flag set.  If two different VFSes with the
8382
** same name are registered, the behavior is undefined.  If a
8383
** VFS is registered with a name that is NULL or an empty string,
8384
** then the behavior is undefined.
8385
**
8386
** ^Unregister a VFS with the sqlite3_vfs_unregister() interface.
8387
** ^(If the default VFS is unregistered, another VFS is chosen as
8388
** the default.  The choice for the new VFS is arbitrary.)^
8389
*/
8390
SQLITE_API sqlite3_vfs *sqlite3_vfs_find(const char *zVfsName);
8391
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_vfs_register(sqlite3_vfs*, int makeDflt);
8392
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_vfs_unregister(sqlite3_vfs*);
8393
8394
/*
8395
** CAPI3REF: Mutexes
8396
**
8397
** The SQLite core uses these routines for thread
8398
** synchronization. Though they are intended for internal
8399
** use by SQLite, code that links against SQLite is
8400
** permitted to use any of these routines.
8401
**
8402
** The SQLite source code contains multiple implementations
8403
** of these mutex routines.  An appropriate implementation
8404
** is selected automatically at compile-time.  The following
8405
** implementations are available in the SQLite core:
8406
**
8407
** <ul>
8408
** <li>   SQLITE_MUTEX_PTHREADS
8409
** <li>   SQLITE_MUTEX_W32
8410
** <li>   SQLITE_MUTEX_NOOP
8411
** </ul>
8412
**
8413
** The SQLITE_MUTEX_NOOP implementation is a set of routines
8414
** that does no real locking and is appropriate for use in
8415
** a single-threaded application.  The SQLITE_MUTEX_PTHREADS and
8416
** SQLITE_MUTEX_W32 implementations are appropriate for use on Unix
8417
** and Windows.
8418
**
8419
**
8420
** ^The sqlite3_mutex_alloc() routine allocates a new
8421
** mutex and returns a pointer to it. ^The sqlite3_mutex_alloc()
8422
** routine returns NULL if it is unable to allocate the requested
8423
** mutex.  The argument to sqlite3_mutex_alloc() must be one of these
8424
** integer constants:
8425
**
8426
** <ul>
8427
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST
8428
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE
8429
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_MAIN
8430
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_MEM
8431
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_OPEN
8432
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_PRNG
8433
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_LRU
8434
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_PMEM
8435
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_APP1
8436
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_APP2
8437
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_APP3
8438
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_VFS1
8439
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_VFS2
8440
** <li>  SQLITE_MUTEX_STATIC_VFS3
8441
** </ul>
8442
**
8443
** ^The first two constants (SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST and SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE)
8444
** cause sqlite3_mutex_alloc() to create
8445
** a new mutex.  ^The new mutex is recursive when SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE
8446
** is used but not necessarily so when SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST is used.
8447
** The mutex implementation does not need to make a distinction
8448
** between SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE and SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST if it does
8449
** not want to.  SQLite will only request a recursive mutex in
8450
** cases where it really needs one.  If a faster non-recursive mutex
8451
** implementation is available on the host platform, the mutex subsystem
8452
** might return such a mutex in response to SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST.
8453
**
8454
** ^The other allowed parameters to sqlite3_mutex_alloc() (anything other
8455
** than SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST and SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE) each return
8456
** a pointer to a static preexisting mutex.  ^Nine static mutexes are
8457
** used by the current version of SQLite.  Future versions of SQLite
8458
** may add additional static mutexes.  Static mutexes are for internal
8459
** use by SQLite only.  Applications that use SQLite mutexes should
8460
** use only the dynamic mutexes returned by SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST or
8461
** SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE.
8462
**
8463
** ^Note that if one of the dynamic mutex parameters (SQLITE_MUTEX_FAST
8464
** or SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE) is used then sqlite3_mutex_alloc()
8465
** returns a different mutex on every call.  ^For the static
8466
** mutex types, the same mutex is returned on every call that has
8467
** the same type number.
8468
**
8469
** ^The sqlite3_mutex_free() routine deallocates a previously
8470
** allocated dynamic mutex.  Attempting to deallocate a static
8471
** mutex results in undefined behavior.
8472
**
8473
** ^The sqlite3_mutex_enter() and sqlite3_mutex_try() routines attempt
8474
** to enter a mutex.  ^If another thread is already within the mutex,
8475
** sqlite3_mutex_enter() will block and sqlite3_mutex_try() will return
8476
** SQLITE_BUSY.  ^The sqlite3_mutex_try() interface returns [SQLITE_OK]
8477
** upon successful entry.  ^(Mutexes created using
8478
** SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE can be entered multiple times by the same thread.
8479
** In such cases, the
8480
** mutex must be exited an equal number of times before another thread
8481
** can enter.)^  If the same thread tries to enter any mutex other
8482
** than an SQLITE_MUTEX_RECURSIVE more than once, the behavior is undefined.
8483
**
8484
** ^(Some systems (for example, Windows 95) do not support the operation
8485
** implemented by sqlite3_mutex_try().  On those systems, sqlite3_mutex_try()
8486
** will always return SQLITE_BUSY. In most cases the SQLite core only uses
8487
** sqlite3_mutex_try() as an optimization, so this is acceptable
8488
** behavior. The exceptions are unix builds that set the
8489
** SQLITE_ENABLE_SETLK_TIMEOUT build option. In that case a working
8490
** sqlite3_mutex_try() is required.)^
8491
**
8492
** ^The sqlite3_mutex_leave() routine exits a mutex that was
8493
** previously entered by the same thread.   The behavior
8494
** is undefined if the mutex is not currently entered by the
8495
** calling thread or is not currently allocated.
8496
**
8497
** ^If the argument to sqlite3_mutex_enter(), sqlite3_mutex_try(),
8498
** sqlite3_mutex_leave(), or sqlite3_mutex_free() is a NULL pointer,
8499
** then any of the four routines behaves as a no-op.
8500
**
8501
** See also: [sqlite3_mutex_held()] and [sqlite3_mutex_notheld()].
8502
*/
8503
SQLITE_API sqlite3_mutex *sqlite3_mutex_alloc(int);
8504
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_mutex_free(sqlite3_mutex*);
8505
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_mutex_enter(sqlite3_mutex*);
8506
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_mutex_try(sqlite3_mutex*);
8507
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_mutex_leave(sqlite3_mutex*);
8508
8509
/*
8510
** CAPI3REF: Mutex Methods Object
8511
**
8512
** An instance of this structure defines the low-level routines
8513
** used to allocate and use mutexes.
8514
**
8515
** Usually, the default mutex implementations provided by SQLite are
8516
** sufficient, however the application has the option of substituting a custom
8517
** implementation for specialized deployments or systems for which SQLite
8518
** does not provide a suitable implementation. In this case, the application
8519
** creates and populates an instance of this structure to pass
8520
** to sqlite3_config() along with the [SQLITE_CONFIG_MUTEX] option.
8521
** Additionally, an instance of this structure can be used as an
8522
** output variable when querying the system for the current mutex
8523
** implementation, using the [SQLITE_CONFIG_GETMUTEX] option.
8524
**
8525
** ^The xMutexInit method defined by this structure is invoked as
8526
** part of system initialization by the sqlite3_initialize() function.
8527
** ^The xMutexInit routine is called by SQLite exactly once for each
8528
** effective call to [sqlite3_initialize()].
8529
**
8530
** ^The xMutexEnd method defined by this structure is invoked as
8531
** part of system shutdown by the sqlite3_shutdown() function. The
8532
** implementation of this method is expected to release all outstanding
8533
** resources obtained by the mutex methods implementation, especially
8534
** those obtained by the xMutexInit method.  ^The xMutexEnd()
8535
** interface is invoked exactly once for each call to [sqlite3_shutdown()].
8536
**
8537
** ^(The remaining seven methods defined by this structure (xMutexAlloc,
8538
** xMutexFree, xMutexEnter, xMutexTry, xMutexLeave, xMutexHeld and
8539
** xMutexNotheld) implement the following interfaces (respectively):
8540
**
8541
** <ul>
8542
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_alloc()] </li>
8543
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_free()] </li>
8544
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_enter()] </li>
8545
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_try()] </li>
8546
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_leave()] </li>
8547
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_held()] </li>
8548
**   <li>  [sqlite3_mutex_notheld()] </li>
8549
** </ul>)^
8550
**
8551
** The only difference is that the public sqlite3_XXX functions enumerated
8552
** above silently ignore any invocations that pass a NULL pointer instead
8553
** of a valid mutex handle. The implementations of the methods defined
8554
** by this structure are not required to handle this case. The results
8555
** of passing a NULL pointer instead of a valid mutex handle are undefined
8556
** (i.e. it is acceptable to provide an implementation that segfaults if
8557
** it is passed a NULL pointer).
8558
**
8559
** The xMutexInit() method must be threadsafe.  It must be harmless to
8560
** invoke xMutexInit() multiple times within the same process and without
8561
** intervening calls to xMutexEnd().  Second and subsequent calls to
8562
** xMutexInit() must be no-ops.
8563
**
8564
** xMutexInit() must not use SQLite memory allocation ([sqlite3_malloc()]
8565
** and its associates).  Similarly, xMutexAlloc() must not use SQLite memory
8566
** allocation for a static mutex.  ^However xMutexAlloc() may use SQLite
8567
** memory allocation for a fast or recursive mutex.
8568
**
8569
** ^SQLite will invoke the xMutexEnd() method when [sqlite3_shutdown()] is
8570
** called, but only if the prior call to xMutexInit returned SQLITE_OK.
8571
** If xMutexInit fails in any way, it is expected to clean up after itself
8572
** prior to returning.
8573
*/
8574
typedef struct sqlite3_mutex_methods sqlite3_mutex_methods;
8575
struct sqlite3_mutex_methods {
8576
  int (*xMutexInit)(void);
8577
  int (*xMutexEnd)(void);
8578
  sqlite3_mutex *(*xMutexAlloc)(int);
8579
  void (*xMutexFree)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8580
  void (*xMutexEnter)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8581
  int (*xMutexTry)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8582
  void (*xMutexLeave)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8583
  int (*xMutexHeld)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8584
  int (*xMutexNotheld)(sqlite3_mutex *);
8585
};
8586
8587
/*
8588
** CAPI3REF: Mutex Verification Routines
8589
**
8590
** The sqlite3_mutex_held() and sqlite3_mutex_notheld() routines
8591
** are intended for use inside assert() statements.  The SQLite core
8592
** never uses these routines except inside an assert() and applications
8593
** are advised to follow the lead of the core.  The SQLite core only
8594
** provides implementations for these routines when it is compiled
8595
** with the SQLITE_DEBUG flag.  External mutex implementations
8596
** are only required to provide these routines if SQLITE_DEBUG is
8597
** defined and if NDEBUG is not defined.
8598
**
8599
** These routines should return true if the mutex in their argument
8600
** is held or not held, respectively, by the calling thread.
8601
**
8602
** The implementation is not required to provide versions of these
8603
** routines that actually work. If the implementation does not provide working
8604
** versions of these routines, it should at least provide stubs that always
8605
** return true so that one does not get spurious assertion failures.
8606
**
8607
** If the argument to sqlite3_mutex_held() is a NULL pointer then
8608
** the routine should return 1.   This seems counter-intuitive since
8609
** clearly the mutex cannot be held if it does not exist.  But
8610
** the reason the mutex does not exist is because the build is not
8611
** using mutexes.  And we do not want the assert() containing the
8612
** call to sqlite3_mutex_held() to fail, so a non-zero return is
8613
** the appropriate thing to do.  The sqlite3_mutex_notheld()
8614
** interface should also return 1 when given a NULL pointer.
8615
*/
8616
#ifndef NDEBUG
8617
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_mutex_held(sqlite3_mutex*);
8618
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_mutex_notheld(sqlite3_mutex*);
8619
#endif

/*
8665
** CAPI3REF: Low-Level Control Of Database Files
8666
** METHOD: sqlite3
8667
** KEYWORDS: {file control}
8668
**
8669
** ^The [sqlite3_file_control()] interface makes a direct call to the
8670
** xFileControl method for the [sqlite3_io_methods] object associated
8671
** with a particular database identified by the second argument. ^The
8672
** name of the database is "main" for the main database or "temp" for the
8673
** TEMP database, or the name that appears after the AS keyword for
8674
** databases that are added using the [ATTACH] SQL command.
8675
** ^A NULL pointer can be used in place of "main" to refer to the
8676
** main database file.
8677
** ^The third and fourth parameters to this routine
8678
** are passed directly through to the second and third parameters of
8679
** the xFileControl method.  ^The return value of the xFileControl
8680
** method becomes the return value of this routine.
8681
**
8682
** A few opcodes for [sqlite3_file_control()] are handled directly
8683
** by the SQLite core and never invoke the
8684
** sqlite3_io_methods.xFileControl method.
8685
** ^The [SQLITE_FCNTL_FILE_POINTER] value for the op parameter causes
8686
** a pointer to the underlying [sqlite3_file] object to be written into
8687
** the space pointed to by the 4th parameter.  The
8688
** [SQLITE_FCNTL_JOURNAL_POINTER] works similarly except that it returns
8689
** the [sqlite3_file] object associated with the journal file instead of
8690
** the main database.  The [SQLITE_FCNTL_VFS_POINTER] opcode returns
8691
** a pointer to the underlying [sqlite3_vfs] object for the file.
8692
** The [SQLITE_FCNTL_DATA_VERSION] returns the data version counter
8693
** from the pager.
8694
**
8695
** ^If the second parameter (zDbName) does not match the name of any
8696
** open database file, then SQLITE_ERROR is returned.  ^This error
8697
** code is not remembered and will not be recalled by [sqlite3_errcode()]
8698
** or [sqlite3_errmsg()].  The underlying xFileControl method might
8699
** also return SQLITE_ERROR.  There is no way to distinguish between
8700
** an incorrect zDbName and an SQLITE_ERROR return from the underlying
8701
** xFileControl method.
8702
**
8703
** See also: [file control opcodes]
8704
*/
8705
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_file_control(sqlite3*, const char *zDbName, int op, void*);

/*
8777
** CAPI3REF: SQL Keyword Checking
8778
**
8779
** These routines provide access to the set of SQL language keywords
8780
** recognized by SQLite.  Applications can use these routines to determine
8781
** whether or not a specific identifier needs to be escaped (for example,
8782
** by enclosing in double-quotes) so as not to confuse the parser.
8783
**
8784
** The sqlite3_keyword_count() interface returns the number of distinct
8785
** keywords understood by SQLite.
8786
**
8787
** The sqlite3_keyword_name(N,Z,L) interface finds the 0-based N-th keyword and
8788
** makes *Z point to that keyword expressed as UTF8 and writes the number
8789
** of bytes in the keyword into *L.  The string that *Z points to is not
8790
** zero-terminated.  The sqlite3_keyword_name(N,Z,L) routine returns
8791
** SQLITE_OK if N is within bounds and SQLITE_ERROR if not. If either Z
8792
** or L are NULL or invalid pointers then calls to
8793
** sqlite3_keyword_name(N,Z,L) result in undefined behavior.
8794
**
8795
** The sqlite3_keyword_check(Z,L) interface checks to see whether or not
8796
** the L-byte UTF8 identifier that Z points to is a keyword, returning non-zero
8797
** if it is and zero if not.
8798
**
8799
** The parser used by SQLite is forgiving.  It is often possible to use
8800
** a keyword as an identifier as long as such use does not result in a
8801
** parsing ambiguity.  For example, the statement
8802
** "CREATE TABLE BEGIN(REPLACE,PRAGMA,END);" is accepted by SQLite, and
8803
** creates a new table named "BEGIN" with three columns named
8804
** "REPLACE", "PRAGMA", and "END".  Nevertheless, best practice is to avoid
8805
** using keywords as identifiers.  Common techniques used to avoid keyword
8806
** name collisions include:
8807
** <ul>
8808
** <li> Put all identifier names inside double-quotes.  This is the official
8809
**      SQL way to escape identifier names.
8810
** <li> Put identifier names inside &#91;...&#93;.  This is not standard SQL,
8811
**      but it is what SQL Server does and so lots of programmers use this
8812
**      technique.
8813
** <li> Begin every identifier with the letter "Z" as no SQL keywords start
8814
**      with "Z".
8815
** <li> Include a digit somewhere in every identifier name.
8816
** </ul>
8817
**
8818
** Note that the number of keywords understood by SQLite can depend on
8819
** compile-time options.  For example, "VACUUM" is not a keyword if
8820
** SQLite is compiled with the [-DSQLITE_OMIT_VACUUM] option.  Also,
8821
** new keywords may be added to future releases of SQLite.
8822
*/
8823
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_keyword_count(void);
8824
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_keyword_name(int,const char**,int*);
8825
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_keyword_check(const char*,int);
8826

/*
8828
** CAPI3REF: Dynamic String Object
8829
** KEYWORDS: {dynamic string}
8830
**
8831
** An instance of the sqlite3_str object contains a dynamically-sized
8832
** string under construction.
8833
**
8834
** The lifecycle of an sqlite3_str object is as follows:
8835
** <ol>
8836
** <li> ^The sqlite3_str object is created using [sqlite3_str_new()].
8837
** <li> ^Text is appended to the sqlite3_str object using various
8838
** methods, such as [sqlite3_str_appendf()].
8839
** <li> The sqlite3_str object is destroyed and the string it created
8840
** is returned using [sqlite3_str_finish()] or [sqlite3_result_str()].
8841
** </ol>
8842
*/
8843
typedef struct sqlite3_str sqlite3_str;
8844
8845
/*
8846
** CAPI3REF: Create A New Dynamic String Object
8847
** CONSTRUCTOR: sqlite3_str
8848
**
8849
** ^The [sqlite3_str_new(D)] interface allocates and initializes
8850
** a new [sqlite3_str] object.  To avoid memory leaks, the object returned by
8851
** [sqlite3_str_new()] must be freed by a subsequent call to
8852
** [sqlite3_str_finish(X)].
8853
**
8854
** ^The [sqlite3_str_new(D)] interface always returns a pointer to a
8855
** valid [sqlite3_str] object, though in the event of an out-of-memory
8856
** error the returned object might be a special singleton that will
8857
** silently reject new text, always return SQLITE_NOMEM from
8858
** [sqlite3_str_errcode()], always return 0 for
8859
** [sqlite3_str_length()], and always return NULL from
8860
** [sqlite3_str_finish(X)].  It is always safe to use the value
8861
** returned by [sqlite3_str_new(D)] as the sqlite3_str parameter
8862
** to any of the other [sqlite3_str] methods.
8863
**
8864
** The D parameter to [sqlite3_str_new(D)] may be NULL.  If the
8865
** D parameter in [sqlite3_str_new(D)] is not NULL, then the maximum
8866
** length of the string contained in the [sqlite3_str] object will be
8867
** the value set for [sqlite3_limit](D,[SQLITE_LIMIT_LENGTH]) instead
8868
** of [SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH].
8869
*/
8870
SQLITE_API sqlite3_str *sqlite3_str_new(sqlite3*);
8871
8872
/*
8873
** CAPI3REF: Finalize A Dynamic String
8874
** DESTRUCTOR: sqlite3_str
8875
**
8876
** ^The [sqlite3_str_finish(X)] interface destroys the sqlite3_str object X
8877
** and returns a pointer to a memory buffer obtained from [sqlite3_malloc64()]
8878
** that contains the constructed string.  The calling application should
8879
** pass the returned value to [sqlite3_free()] to avoid a memory leak.
8880
** ^The [sqlite3_str_finish(X)] interface may return a NULL pointer if any
8881
** errors were encountered during construction of the string.  ^The
8882
** [sqlite3_str_finish(X)] interface might also return a NULL pointer if the
8883
** string in [sqlite3_str] object X is zero bytes long.
8884
**
8885
** ^The [sqlite3_str_free(X)] interface destroys both the sqlite3_str object
8886
** X and the string content it contains.  Calling sqlite3_str_free(X) is
8887
** the equivalent of calling [sqlite3_free](sqlite3_str_finish(X)).
8888
*/
8889
SQLITE_API char *sqlite3_str_finish(sqlite3_str*);
8890
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_free(sqlite3_str*);
8891
8892
/*
8893
** CAPI3REF: Return A Dynamic String From an SQL Function
8894
**
8895
** The [sqlite3_result_str(C,S,F)] interface causes the
8896
** [sqlite3_str|dynamic string] S to become the return value for the
8897
** application-defined function or virtual table that uses
8898
** [sqlite3_context] C.  The F flag can be one of [SQLITE_COPY]
8899
** or [SQLITE_XFER] or [SQLITE_FINISH].
8900
**
8901
** If the dynamic string is invalid or incomplete due to an out-of-memory
8902
** or string-too-large error, then this routine transfers that error
8903
** over to the SQL function.
8904
**
8905
** If the F argument is SQLITE_COPY, then a copy of the dynamic string
8906
** content is made and the dynamic string object is unchanged.
8907
** If the F argument is SQLITE_XFER, then ownership of the content
8908
** in the dynamic is transferred to the SQL function (via a pointer copy
8909
** rather than a string copy) and the dynamic string is reset to an
8910
** empty string.  The SQLITE_FINISH value for F works like SQLITE_RESET
8911
** except that it also invokes the [sqlite3_str_free(S)] destructor
8912
** on the dynamic string object.
8913
*/
8914
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_result_str(sqlite3_context*, sqlite3_str*, int);
8915
8916
/*
8917
** CAPI3REF: Control Flags For sqlite3_result_str()
8918
**
8919
** The following integers can be used as the third "F" argument
8920
** to [sqlite3_result_str(C,S,F)].
8921
*/
8922
#define SQLITE_COPY   0   /* Results copied.  Dynamic string unchanged */
8923
#define SQLITE_XFER   1   /* Results transfered.  Dynamic string reset */
8924
#define SQLITE_FINISH 2   /* Like SQLITE_XFER, plus dynamic string freed */
8925
8926
/*
8927
** CAPI3REF: Add Content To A Dynamic String
8928
** METHOD: sqlite3_str
8929
**
8930
** These interfaces add or remove content to an sqlite3_str object
8931
** previously obtained from [sqlite3_str_new()].
8932
**
8933
** ^The [sqlite3_str_appendf(X,F,...)] and
8934
** [sqlite3_str_vappendf(X,F,V)] interfaces uses the [built-in printf]
8935
** functionality of SQLite to append formatted text onto the end of
8936
** [sqlite3_str] object X.
8937
**
8938
** ^The [sqlite3_str_append(X,S,N)] method appends exactly N bytes from string S
8939
** onto the end of the [sqlite3_str] object X.  N must be non-negative.
8940
** S must contain at least N non-zero bytes of content.  To append a
8941
** zero-terminated string in its entirety, use the [sqlite3_str_appendall()]
8942
** method instead.
8943
**
8944
** ^The [sqlite3_str_appendall(X,S)] method appends the complete content of
8945
** zero-terminated string S onto the end of [sqlite3_str] object X.
8946
**
8947
** ^The [sqlite3_str_appendchar(X,N,C)] method appends N copies of the
8948
** single-byte character C onto the end of [sqlite3_str] object X.
8949
** ^This method can be used, for example, to add whitespace indentation.
8950
**
8951
** ^The [sqlite3_str_reset(X)] method resets the string under construction
8952
** inside [sqlite3_str] object X back to zero bytes in length.
8953
**
8954
** ^The [sqlite3_str_truncate(X,N)] method changes the length of the string
8955
** under construction to be N bytes or less.  This routine is a no-op if
8956
** N is negative or if the string is already N bytes or smaller in size.
8957
**
8958
** These methods do not return a result code.  ^If an error occurs, that fact
8959
** is recorded in the [sqlite3_str] object and can be recovered by a
8960
** subsequent call to [sqlite3_str_errcode(X)].
8961
*/
8962
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_appendf(sqlite3_str*, const char *zFormat, ...);
8963
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_vappendf(sqlite3_str*, const char *zFormat, va_list);
8964
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_append(sqlite3_str*, const char *zIn, int N);
8965
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_appendall(sqlite3_str*, const char *zIn);
8966
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_appendchar(sqlite3_str*, int N, char C);
8967
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_reset(sqlite3_str*);
8968
SQLITE_API void sqlite3_str_truncate(sqlite3_str*,int N);
8969
8970
/*
8971
** CAPI3REF: Status Of A Dynamic String
8972
** METHOD: sqlite3_str
8973
**
8974
** These interfaces return the current status of an [sqlite3_str] object.
8975
**
8976
** ^If any prior errors have occurred while constructing the dynamic string
8977
** in sqlite3_str X, then the [sqlite3_str_errcode(X)] method will return
8978
** an appropriate error code.  ^The [sqlite3_str_errcode(X)] method returns
8979
** [SQLITE_NOMEM] following any out-of-memory error, or
8980
** [SQLITE_TOOBIG] if the size of the dynamic string exceeds
8981
** [SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH], or [SQLITE_OK] if there have been no errors.
8982
**
8983
** ^The [sqlite3_str_length(X)] method returns the current length, in bytes,
8984
** of the dynamic string under construction in [sqlite3_str] object X.
8985
** ^The length returned by [sqlite3_str_length(X)] does not include the
8986
** zero-termination byte.
8987
**
8988
** ^The [sqlite3_str_value(X)] method returns a pointer to the current
8989
** content of the dynamic string under construction in X.  The value
8990
** returned by [sqlite3_str_value(X)] is managed by the sqlite3_str object X
8991
** and might be freed or altered by any subsequent method on the same
8992
** [sqlite3_str] object.  Applications must not use the pointer returned by
8993
** [sqlite3_str_value(X)] after any subsequent method call on the same
8994
** object.  ^Applications may change the content of the string returned
8995
** by [sqlite3_str_value(X)] as long as they do not write into any bytes
8996
** outside the range of 0 to [sqlite3_str_length(X)] and do not read or
8997
** write any byte after any subsequent sqlite3_str method call.
8998
*/
8999
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_str_errcode(sqlite3_str*);
9000
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_str_length(sqlite3_str*);
9001
SQLITE_API char *sqlite3_str_value(sqlite3_str*);
9002
9003
/*
9004
** CAPI3REF: SQLite Runtime Status
9005
**
9006
** ^These interfaces are used to retrieve runtime status information
9007
** about the performance of SQLite, and optionally to reset various
9008
** highwater marks.  ^The first argument is an integer code for
9009
** the specific parameter to measure.  ^(Recognized integer codes
9010
** are of the form [status parameters | SQLITE_STATUS_...].)^
9011
** ^The current value of the parameter is returned into *pCurrent.
9012
** ^The highest recorded value is returned in *pHighwater.  ^If the
9013
** resetFlag is true, then the highest record value is reset after
9014
** *pHighwater is written.  ^(Some parameters do not record the highest
9015
** value.  For those parameters
9016
** nothing is written into *pHighwater and the resetFlag is ignored.)^
9017
** ^(Other parameters record only the highwater mark and not the current
9018
** value.  For these latter parameters nothing is written into *pCurrent.)^
9019
**
9020
** ^The sqlite3_status() and sqlite3_status64() routines return
9021
** SQLITE_OK on success and a non-zero [error code] on failure.
9022
**
9023
** If either the current value or the highwater mark is too large to
9024
** be represented by a 32-bit integer, then the values returned by
9025
** sqlite3_status() are undefined.
9026
**
9027
** See also: [sqlite3_db_status()]
9028
*/
9029
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_status(int op, int *pCurrent, int *pHighwater, int resetFlag);
9030
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_status64(
9031
  int op,
9032
  sqlite3_int64 *pCurrent,
9033
  sqlite3_int64 *pHighwater,
9034
  int resetFlag
9035
);

/*
9039
** CAPI3REF: Status Parameters
9040
** KEYWORDS: {status parameters}
9041
**
9042
** These integer constants designate various run-time status parameters
9043
** that can be returned by [sqlite3_status()].
9044
**
9045
** <dl>
9046
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_MEMORY_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_MEMORY_USED</dt>
9047
** <dd>This parameter is the current amount of memory checked out
9048
** using [sqlite3_malloc()], either directly or indirectly.  The
9049
** figure includes calls made to [sqlite3_malloc()] by the application
9050
** and internal memory usage by the SQLite library.  Auxiliary page-cache
9051
** memory controlled by [SQLITE_CONFIG_PAGECACHE] is not included in
9052
** this parameter.  The amount returned is the sum of the allocation
9053
** sizes as reported by the xSize method in [sqlite3_mem_methods].</dd>)^
9054
**
9055
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_SIZE]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_SIZE</dt>
9056
** <dd>This parameter records the largest memory allocation request
9057
** handed to [sqlite3_malloc()] or [sqlite3_realloc()] (or their
9058
** internal equivalents).  Only the value returned in the
9059
** *pHighwater parameter to [sqlite3_status()] is of interest.
9060
** The value written into the *pCurrent parameter is undefined.</dd>)^
9061
**
9062
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT</dt>
9063
** <dd>This parameter records the number of separate memory allocations
9064
** currently checked out.</dd>)^
9065
**
9066
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_USED</dt>
9067
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of pages used out of the
9068
** [pagecache memory allocator] that was configured using
9069
** [SQLITE_CONFIG_PAGECACHE].  The
9070
** value returned is in pages, not in bytes.</dd>)^
9071
**
9072
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_OVERFLOW]]
9073
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_OVERFLOW</dt>
9074
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of bytes of page cache
9075
** allocation which could not be satisfied by the [SQLITE_CONFIG_PAGECACHE]
9076
** buffer and where forced to overflow to [sqlite3_malloc()].  The
9077
** returned value includes allocations that overflowed because they
9078
** were too large (they were larger than the "sz" parameter to
9079
** [SQLITE_CONFIG_PAGECACHE]) and allocations that overflowed because
9080
** no space was left in the page cache.</dd>)^
9081
**
9082
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_SIZE]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_SIZE</dt>
9083
** <dd>This parameter records the largest memory allocation request
9084
** handed to the [pagecache memory allocator].  Only the value returned in the
9085
** *pHighwater parameter to [sqlite3_status()] is of interest.
9086
** The value written into the *pCurrent parameter is undefined.</dd>)^
9087
**
9088
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_USED]] <dt>SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_USED</dt>
9089
** <dd>No longer used.</dd>
9090
**
9091
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_OVERFLOW]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_OVERFLOW</dt>
9092
** <dd>No longer used.</dd>
9093
**
9094
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_SIZE]] <dt>SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_SIZE</dt>
9095
** <dd>No longer used.</dd>
9096
**
9097
** [[SQLITE_STATUS_PARSER_STACK]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_STATUS_PARSER_STACK</dt>
9098
** <dd>The *pHighwater parameter records the deepest parser stack.
9099
** The *pCurrent value is undefined.  The *pHighwater value is only
9100
** meaningful if SQLite is compiled with [YYTRACKMAXSTACKDEPTH].</dd>)^
9101
** </dl>
9102
**
9103
** New status parameters may be added from time to time.
9104
*/
9105
#define SQLITE_STATUS_MEMORY_USED          0
9106
#define SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_USED       1
9107
#define SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_OVERFLOW   2
9108
#define SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_USED         3  /* NOT USED */
9109
#define SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_OVERFLOW     4  /* NOT USED */
9110
#define SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_SIZE          5
9111
#define SQLITE_STATUS_PARSER_STACK         6
9112
#define SQLITE_STATUS_PAGECACHE_SIZE       7
9113
#define SQLITE_STATUS_SCRATCH_SIZE         8  /* NOT USED */
9114
#define SQLITE_STATUS_MALLOC_COUNT         9

/*
9117
** CAPI3REF: Database Connection Status
9118
** METHOD: sqlite3
9119
**
9120
** ^This interface is used to retrieve runtime status information
9121
** about a single [database connection].  ^The first argument is the
9122
** database connection object to be interrogated.  ^The second argument
9123
** is an integer constant, taken from the set of
9124
** [SQLITE_DBSTATUS options], that
9125
** determines the parameter to interrogate.  The set of
9126
** [SQLITE_DBSTATUS options] is likely
9127
** to grow in future releases of SQLite.
9128
**
9129
** ^The current value of the requested parameter is written into *pCur
9130
** and the highest instantaneous value is written into *pHiwtr.  ^If
9131
** the resetFlg is true, then the highest instantaneous value is
9132
** reset back down to the current value.
9133
**
9134
** ^The sqlite3_db_status() routine returns SQLITE_OK on success and a
9135
** non-zero [error code] on failure.
9136
**
9137
** ^The sqlite3_db_status64(D,O,C,H,R) routine works exactly the same
9138
** way as sqlite3_db_status(D,O,C,H,R) routine except that the C and H
9139
** parameters are pointer to 64-bit integers (type: sqlite3_int64) instead
9140
** of pointers to 32-bit integers, which allows larger status values
9141
** to be returned.  If a status value exceeds 2,147,483,647 then
9142
** sqlite3_db_status() will truncate the value whereas sqlite3_db_status64()
9143
** will return the full value.
9144
**
9145
** See also: [sqlite3_status()] and [sqlite3_stmt_status()].
9146
*/
9147
SQLITE_API int sqlite3_db_status(sqlite3*, int op, int *pCur, int *pHiwtr, int resetFlg);

SQLITE_API int sqlite3_db_status64(sqlite3*,int,sqlite3_int64*,sqlite3_int64*,int);

/*
9151
** CAPI3REF: Status Parameters for database connections
9152
** KEYWORDS: {SQLITE_DBSTATUS options}
9153
**
9154
** These constants are the available integer "verbs" that can be passed as
9155
** the second argument to the [sqlite3_db_status()] interface.
9156
**
9157
** New verbs may be added in future releases of SQLite. Existing verbs
9158
** might be discontinued. Applications should check the return code from
9159
** [sqlite3_db_status()] to make sure that the call worked.
9160
** The [sqlite3_db_status()] interface will return a non-zero error code
9161
** if a discontinued or unsupported verb is invoked.
9162
**
9163
** <dl>
9164
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_USED</dt>
9165
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of lookaside memory slots currently
9166
** checked out.</dd>)^
9167
**
9168
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_HIT]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_HIT</dt>
9169
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of malloc attempts that were
9170
** satisfied using lookaside memory. Only the high-water value is meaningful;
9171
** the current value is always zero.</dd>)^
9172
**
9173
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_SIZE]]
9174
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_SIZE</dt>
9175
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of malloc attempts that might have
9176
** been satisfied using lookaside memory but failed due to the amount of
9177
** memory requested being larger than the lookaside slot size.
9178
** Only the high-water value is meaningful;
9179
** the current value is always zero.</dd>)^
9180
**
9181
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_FULL]]
9182
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_FULL</dt>
9183
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of malloc attempts that might have
9184
** been satisfied using lookaside memory but failed due to all lookaside
9185
** memory already being in use.
9186
** Only the high-water value is meaningful;
9187
** the current value is always zero.</dd>)^
9188
**
9189
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED</dt>
9190
** <dd>This parameter returns the approximate number of bytes of heap
9191
** memory used by all pager caches associated with the database connection.)^
9192
** ^The highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED is always 0.
9193
** </dd>
9194
**
9195
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED_SHARED]]
9196
** ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED_SHARED</dt>
9197
** <dd>This parameter is similar to DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED, except that if a
9198
** pager cache is shared between two or more connections the bytes of heap
9199
** memory used by that pager cache is divided evenly between the attached
9200
** connections.)^  In other words, if none of the pager caches associated
9201
** with the database connection are shared, this request returns the same
9202
** value as DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED. Or, if one or more of the pager caches are
9203
** shared, the value returned by this call will be smaller than that returned
9204
** by DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED. ^The highwater mark associated with
9205
** SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED_SHARED is always 0.</dd>
9206
**
9207
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_SCHEMA_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_SCHEMA_USED</dt>
9208
** <dd>This parameter returns the approximate number of bytes of heap
9209
** memory used to store the schema for all databases associated
9210
** with the connection - main, temp, and any [ATTACH]-ed databases.)^
9211
** ^The full amount of memory used by the schemas is reported, even if the
9212
** schema memory is shared with other database connections due to
9213
** [shared cache mode] being enabled.
9214
** ^The highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_SCHEMA_USED is always 0.
9215
** </dd>
9216
**
9217
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_STMT_USED]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_STMT_USED</dt>
9218
** <dd>This parameter returns the approximate number of bytes of heap
9219
** and lookaside memory used by all prepared statements associated with
9220
** the database connection.)^
9221
** ^The highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_STMT_USED is always 0.
9222
** </dd>
9223
**
9224
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_HIT]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_HIT</dt>
9225
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of pager cache hits that have
9226
** occurred.)^ ^The highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_HIT
9227
** is always 0.
9228
** </dd>
9229
**
9230
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_MISS]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_MISS</dt>
9231
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of pager cache misses that have
9232
** occurred.)^ ^The highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_MISS
9233
** is always 0.
9234
** </dd>
9235
**
9236
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE</dt>
9237
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of dirty cache entries that have
9238
** been written to disk. Specifically, the number of pages written to the
9239
** wal file in wal mode databases, or the number of pages written to the
9240
** database file in rollback mode databases. Any pages written as part of
9241
** transaction rollback or database recovery operations are not included.
9242
** If an IO or other error occurs while writing a page to disk, the effect
9243
** on subsequent SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE requests is undefined.)^ ^The
9244
** highwater mark associated with SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE is always 0.
9245
** <p>
9246
** ^(There is overlap between the quantities measured by this parameter
9247
** (SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE) and SQLITE_DBSTATUS_TEMPBUF_SPILL.
9248
** Resetting one will reduce the other.)^
9249
** </dd>
9250
**
9251
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_SPILL]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_SPILL</dt>
9252
** <dd>This parameter returns the number of dirty cache entries that have
9253
** been written to disk in the middle of a transaction due to the page
9254
** cache overflowing. Transactions are more efficient if they are written
9255
** to disk all at once. When pages spill mid-transaction, that introduces
9256
** additional overhead. This parameter can be used to help identify
9257
** inefficiencies that can be resolved by increasing the cache size.
9258
** </dd>
9259
**
9260
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_DEFERRED_FKS]] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_DEFERRED_FKS</dt>
9261
** <dd>This parameter returns zero for the current value if and only if
9262
** all foreign key constraints (deferred or immediate) have been
9263
** resolved.)^  ^The highwater mark is always 0.
9264
**
9265
** [[SQLITE_DBSTATUS_TEMPBUF_SPILL] ^(<dt>SQLITE_DBSTATUS_TEMPBUF_SPILL</dt>
9266
** <dd>^(This parameter returns the number of bytes written to temporary
9267
** files on disk that could have been kept in memory had sufficient memory
9268
** been available.  This value includes writes to intermediate tables that
9269
** are part of complex queries, external sorts that spill to disk, and
9270
** writes to TEMP tables.)^
9271
** ^The highwater mark is always 0.
9272
** <p>
9273
** ^(There is overlap between the quantities measured by this parameter
9274
** (SQLITE_DBSTATUS_TEMPBUF_SPILL) and SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE.
9275
** Resetting one will reduce the other.)^
9276
** </dd>
9277
** </dl>
9278
*/
9279
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_USED       0
9280
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED           1
9281
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_SCHEMA_USED          2
9282
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_STMT_USED            3
9283
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_HIT        4
9284
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_SIZE  5
9285
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_LOOKASIDE_MISS_FULL  6
9286
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_HIT            7
9287
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_MISS           8
9288
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_WRITE          9
9289
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_DEFERRED_FKS        10
9290
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_USED_SHARED   11
9291
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_CACHE_SPILL         12
9292
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_TEMPBUF_SPILL       13
9293
#define SQLITE_DBSTATUS_MAX                 13   /* Largest defined DBSTATUS */
9294
